Classification Accuracy and Consistency
text: many testing contexts, test scores used assign examinees performance categories, example, pass/fail decisions placement proficiency levels. Two indices quantify quality classification decisions: Classification Accuracy (CA): probability examinee correctly classified based true latent ability. Classification Consistency (CC): probability classification result two independent administrations test. indices essential supporting valid score interpretations high-stakes settings. data repeated test administrations rarely available, single-administration estimation procedures based IRT models commonly used. irtQ implements two IRT-based estimation methods: functions support two estimation approaches: D-method (distribution-based): integrates conditional indices population ability distribution specified quadrature points weights. approach appropriate empirical ability distribution (e.g., posterior quadrature weights IRT calibration) available. P-method (person-based): averages conditional indices individual ability estimates sample examinees. functions return list five elements: $confusion: confusion matrix (rows = true level, columns = expected level), $marginal: data frame one row per true performance level overall marginal row. level row contribution examinees true level, level rows add overall marginal CA CC, $conditional: data frame conditional CA CC theta (node), $prob.level: data frame probability assigned level theta (node), $cutscore: cut scores used analysis (observed score scale cac_lee() theta scale cac_rud()).

This mirrors the example used in `?ctt` flex_sam <- system.file("extdata", "flexmirt_sample-prm.txt", package = "irtQ") x <- bring.flexmirt(file = flex_sam, "par")$Group1$full_df set.seed(2026) theta <- rnorm(1000) dat_mixed <- simdat(x = x, theta = theta, D = 1)  dim(dat_mixed)   # 1,000 examinees x 55 items #> [1] 1000   55 table(x$cats)    # 50 items with cats = 2 (dichotomous), 5 items with cats = 5 (GRM) #>  #>  2  5  #> 50  5  # Data set 2: a small dichotomous-only response matrix (300 examinees on 15 # simulated 3PLM items), used for a simpler, easier-to-read walk-through of # ctt()'s item- and test-level output set.seed(1) x_bin <- shape_df(   par.drm = list(a = rep(1.5, 15), b = seq(-1.5, 1.5, length.out = 15),                  g = rep(0.2, 15)),   cats = 2, model = "3PLM" ) dat_bin <- simdat(x = x_bin, theta = rnorm(300), D = 1) dim(dat_bin)     # 300 examinees x 15 items #> [1] 300  15

title: DIF Detection
text: simulate 40-item dichotomous test (3PLM) 1,000 examinees per group. DIF introduced six items: Items 1-2: Uniform DIF, focal group higher difficulty parameter (b+0.5b + 0.5) discrimination parameter unchanged. Items 3-4: Nonuniform DIF, focal group lower discrimination parameter (×0.5a \times 0.5) difficulty parameter unchanged. Items 5-6: Mixed DIF, focal group lower discrimination parameter (×0.5a \times 0.5) higher difficulty parameter (b+0.5b + 0.5), making items less discriminating harder focal group. Items 7-40: DIF. focal group slightly lower mean ability (μ=−0.3\mu = -0.3) reference group (μ=0\mu = 0), representing realistic impact condition. item difficulties drawn U(−2.5,2.5)U(-2.5, 2.5). Items extremely easy hard examinees can make pooled calibration unstable, range kept moderate. Next, calibrate item parameters using pooled data estimate ability scores. RDIF framework requires ability estimates based pooled (aggregate) item parameters, calibration scoring must performed combined data regardless group membership (Lim et al., 2022). element test.1 calibration result reports whether EM algorithm converged; checked estimates used.
code: J   <- 40     # number of items N_R <- 1000   # reference group size N_F <- 1000   # focal group size  # Base item parameters (no DIF) shared by both groups set.seed(123) a_base <- round(runif(J, 0.7, 1.7), 2) b_base <- round(runif(J, -2.5, 2.5), 2) g_base <- rep(0.15, J)  # Reference group item metadata (no DIF) meta_ref <- shape_df(   par.drm = list(a = a_base, b = b_base, g = g_base),   cats    = 2,   model   = "3PLM" )  # Focal group item metadata: DIF injected into items 1-6 a_focal      <- a_base b_focal      <- b_base b_focal[1:2] <- b_base[1:2] + 0.5          # uniform DIF: harder for focal a_focal[3:4] <- a_base[3:4] * 0.5          # nonuniform DIF: less discriminating a_focal[5:6] <- a_base[5:6] * 0.5          # mixed DIF: less discriminating ... b_focal[5:6] <- b_base[5:6] + 0.5          # ... and harder for focal  meta_foc <- shape_df(   par.drm = list(a = a_focal, b = b_focal, g = g_base),   cats    = 2,   model   = "3PLM" )  # Simulate ability parameters: reference N(0,1), focal N(-0.3,1) theta_R <- rnorm(N_R, mean =  0.0, sd = 1) theta_F <- rnorm(N_F, mean = -0.3, sd = 1)  # Simulate item responses separately for each group resp_R <- simdat(x = meta_ref, theta = theta_R, D = 1.702) resp_F <- simdat(x = meta_foc, theta = theta_F, D = 1.702)  # Pool responses and define group membership vector (0 = reference, 1 = focal) resp_pool <- rbind(resp_R, resp_F) group_vec <- c(rep(0, N_R), rep(1, N_F))  cat("Pooled data:", nrow(resp_pool), "examinees x", ncol(resp_pool), "items\n") #> Pooled data: 2000 examinees x 40 items # Calibrate item parameters from the pooled data mod_pool <- est_irt(   data       = resp_pool,   D          = 1.702,   model      = "3PLM",   cats       = 2,   use.gprior = TRUE,   gprior     = list(dist = "beta", params = c(4, 16)),   EmpHist    = TRUE,   MaxE       = 1000,    # allow extra EM cycles   verbose    = FALSE )  # Check that the EM algorithm converged mod_pool$test.1 #> [1] "Convergence criteria are satisfied."  meta_pool <- mod_pool$par.est  # Estimate ability using ML method # ML is recommended for RDIF analysis as it provides point estimates # unaffected by prior distribution assumptions (Lim et al., 2022) score_pool <- est_score(   x      = meta_pool,   data   = resp_pool,   D      = 1.702,   method = "ML",   range  = c(-5, 5) )$est.theta

text: using irtQ, helps understand IRT preferred Classical Test Theory (CTT) many measurement tasks. Classical Test Theory (CTT) summarizes examinees total (proportion) correct score items observed difficulty (p-value) point-biserial correlation. straightforward, CTT well-known limitations: Sample dependence: item statistics (difficulty, discrimination) change examinee group, person scores change item set item-level probability model: CTT tell us probability specific person answers specific item correctly Limited equating: comparing scores across different test forms requires strong assumptions Item Response Theory (IRT) addresses limitations modeling probability response function latent trait θ\theta (ability, proficiency, attitude) item parameters. Key advantages : Invariance: item parameters depend ability distribution calibration sample; person parameters depend particular items administered Item-level modeling: item characteristic curve describing response probability changes θ\theta Common scale: items persons placed θ\theta continuum, enabling equating, adaptive testing, longitudinal measurement

title: Getting Started: A Detailed Guide
text: irtQ covers full IRT workflow: Primary functions: Estimating item parameters: fixed-form calibration, pretest calibration using Fixed Item Parameter Calibration (FIPC) Fixed Ability Parameter Calibration (FAPC) approaches, multiple-group calibration (est_irt(), est_mg(), est_item()) Estimating examinee abilities: maximum likelihood (ML), maximum likelihood fences (MLF), weighted likelihood (WL), maximum posteriori (MAP), expected posteriori (EAP), EAP summed scoring, inverse test characteristic curve (TCC) scoring (est_score()) Evaluating item-level model-data fit: χ2\chi^2, G2G^2, infit/outfit, SS-X2X^2 (irtfit(), sx2_fit()) Detecting differential item functioning (DIF): residual-based DIF (RDIF), generalized residual-based DIF (GRDIF), simultaneous item bias test modified CAT (CATSIB) (rdif(), grdif(), catsib()) Detecting item parameter drift (IPD): residual-based IPD (RIPD) pseudo-count D2D^2 statistic (ripd(), pcd2()) Computing classification accuracy consistency indices (cac_lee(), cac_rud()) Evaluating simulating multistage-adaptive test (MST) panels: panel structure, routing cut scores, recursion-based evaluation, simulation (panel_info(), find_cut(), reval_mst(), run_mst()) Beyond IRT-based analyses, irtQ also provides small set classical test theory (CTT) functions (item difficulty, item-total correlation, Cronbach’s alpha, option/distractor response distributions, total-score frequency distributions) scoring analyzing selected-response item data without fitting IRT model (ctt(), freq_score(), ctt_distr(), score_resp()). Utilities: article introduces IRT models supported irtQ item metadata data structure connects functions. end, minimal end--end workflow ties everything together.

Parameters: aa: single discrimination parameter item b1,b2,…,bK−1b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_{K-1}: step parameters (also called threshold parameters), bvb_v governs transition category v−1v-1 category vv. Unlike GRM thresholds, GPCM step parameters need ordered. Relationship models: Setting =1a = 1 items gives Partial Credit Model (PCM) (Masters, 1982) GPCM therefore generalization PCM allows item-varying discrimination irtQ, PCM item specified model = "GPCM" fix..gpcm = TRUE (.val.gpcm = 1) estimation functions; D = 1 latent variance fixed 1 (default), PCM. separate "PCM" model string. specify irtQ: item KK categories, provide vector K−1K - 1 step parameters d argument shape_df(). v=0v = 0 term handled internally; supply b0b_0.

title: Introduction to irtQ
text: irtQ package fits unidimensional item response theory (IRT) models test data may contain dichotomous polytomous items. dichotomous models one-, two-, three-parameter logistic models (1PLM, 2PLM, 3PLM), polytomous models graded response model (GRM) generalized partial credit model (GPCM). single test can mix models. package covers steps typical IRT analysis: estimating item parameters marginal maximum likelihood EM algorithm (est_irt(), est_mg()), calibrating pretest items fixed item parameters fixed abilities (est_irt(), est_item()), estimating examinees’ abilities (est_score()), evaluating model-data fit (irtfit(), sx2_fit()), detecting differential item functioning (rdif(), crdif(), grdif(), catsib()) item parameter drift (ripd(), pcd2()). also provides functions item test information (info()), item response curves (traceline()), classification accuracy consistency (cac_lee(), cac_rud()), multistage test panels (panel_info(), find_cut(), reval_mst(), run_mst()), classical test theory (ctt(), freq_score(), ctt_distr(), score_resp()). vignette walks short workflow: read item parameters, simulate responses, calibrate items, estimate abilities, check fit, compute test information. Every example uses scaling constant D = 1.

title: Introduction to irtQ
text: irtQ functions take data frame item metadata first argument, fitted object contains one. row describes one item. Item metadata can read output IRT software bring.*() functions (bring.flexmirt(), bring.bilog(), bring.parscale(), bring.mirt(), requires suggested mirt package) created shape_df(). example reads flexMIRT parameter file ships package keeps first 25 items, follow 3PLM. small metadata frame can also written directly shape_df().

title: Item Parameter Estimation
text: est_irt() function implements Marginal Maximum Likelihood Estimation via Expectation-Maximization (MMLE-EM) algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981). avoid incidental parameter problem (estimating individual ability θ\theta leads inconsistent item parameter estimates sample size grows), algorithm treats θ\theta random variable following specific prior distribution, typically g(θ)∼N(0,1)g(\theta) \sim N(0, 1). Note Item Types: clarity simplicity, mathematical formulation explanations presented using dichotomous (binary) items, although underlying logic extends polytomous item response models. integrating latent variable θ\theta joint likelihood, obtain marginal log-likelihood observed data, item parameters (𝚫\boldsymbol{\Delta}) parameters estimated: log⁡L(𝚫∣𝐔)=∑=1Nlog⁡∫−∞∞L(𝐮i∣θ)g(θ)dθ \log L(\boldsymbol{\Delta} \mid \mathbf{U}) = \sum_{=1}^{N} \log \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} L(\mathbf{u}_i \mid \theta)\, g(\theta) d\theta L(𝐮i∣θ)L(\mathbf{u}_i \mid \theta) likelihood observing examinee ii’s response pattern 𝐮i\mathbf{u}_i given ability θ\theta, g(θ)g(\theta) prior density function latent ability. Using KK-point quadrature, continuous integral approximated discrete summation KK quadrature points θk\theta_k prior weights wkw_k (weights standard normal distribution): log⁡Lmarginal(𝚫∣𝐔)≈∑=1Nlog⁡∑k=1KL(𝐮i∣θk)wk \log L_{marginal}(\boldsymbol{\Delta} \mid \mathbf{U}) \approx \sum_{=1}^{N} \log \sum_{k=1}^{K} L(\mathbf{u}_i \mid \theta_k)\, w_k maximize marginal log-likelihood, analytically intractable due summation inside logarithm, est_irt() iteratively executes following E-step M-step convergence: E-step (Expectation): Computing Artificial Sufficient Statistics examinee response pattern 𝐮i\mathbf{u}_i, algorithm first computes posterior probability θ\theta quadrature point θk\theta_k: P(θk∣𝐮i)=L(𝐮i∣θk)wk∑m=1KL(𝐮i∣θm)wm P(\theta_k \mid \mathbf{u}_i) = \frac{L(\mathbf{u}_i \mid \theta_k)\, w_k}{\sum_{m=1}^{K} L(\mathbf{u}_i \mid \theta_m)\, w_m} Using individual posteriors, algorithm aggregates data across NN examinees construct artificial sufficient statistics quadrature point: Expected number examinees (nkn_k) θk\theta_k: nk=∑=1NP(θk∣𝐮i) n_k = \sum_{=1}^{N} P(\theta_k \mid \mathbf{u}_i) Expected number correct responses (rjkr_{jk}) item jj θk\theta_k: rjk=∑=1NuijP(θk∣𝐮i) r_{jk} = \sum_{=1}^{N} u_{ij} P(\theta_k \mid \mathbf{u}_i) M-step (Maximization): Item--Item Parameter Optimization M-step, algorithm treats nkn_k rjkr_{jk} fixed constants. decoupling joint likelihood, parameters item jj can updated independently (item--item) maximizing expected complete-data log-likelihood (QQ-function): ℓj(𝛅j)=∑k=1K[rjklnPj(θk)+(nk−rjk)ln(1−Pj(θk))] \ell_j(\boldsymbol{\delta}_j) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \left[ r_{jk} \ln P_j(\theta_k) + (n_k - r_{jk}) \ln (1 - P_j(\theta_k)) \right] 𝛅j\boldsymbol{\delta}_j denotes item parameter vector (e.g., slope aja_j difficulty bjb_j 2PL model) Pj(θk)P_j(\theta_k) item response function. est_irt() maximizes function item stats::nlminb() using analytic gradients Hessians. priors specified item parameters, log prior densities added function, estimates Bayes modal estimates. Extension Polytomous Items: formulation uses dichotomous items ease illustration, underlying MMLE-EM framework generalizes polytomous item response models (e.g., Graded Response Model, Generalized Partial Credit Model). polytomous items, expected complete-data log-likelihood incorporates multinomial category response probabilities Pjv(θk)P_{jv}(\theta_k) corresponding expected category frequencies rjvkr_{jvk} category vv, maintaining identical decoupling optimization structure. Convergence two-step cycle (E M) repeats. algorithm terminates maximum absolute change item parameter estimates consecutive EM cycles less equal convergence threshold specified Etol argument. mean variance latent distribution estimated FIPC weights empirical histogram part criterion; smaller Etol gives precise values . Key advantages MMLE-EM: require individual ability estimates (θ\theta “integrated ”) Handles missing responses omitting likelihood (assuming missing random) Allows prior distributions item parameters numerical stability

title: Item Parameter Estimation
text: 1-parameter logistic model (1PLM) simplest IRT model dichotomous items. assumes: items equal discrimination (slopes) Items differ difficulty (location) guessing (lower asymptote = 0) Mathematical form: P(Y=1∣θ)=11+exp⁡(−D⋅⋅(θ−b)) P(Y = 1 \mid \theta) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-D \cdot \cdot (\theta - b))} aa constrained equal across items (fixed 1). Two ways fit 1PLM irtQ: fix..1pl = TRUE: Fix aa .val.1pl (1) 1PLM items fix..1pl = FALSE (default): Constrain aa equal across 1PLM items estimate common value data cases latent distribution fixed N(0, 1) (group.mean = 0, group.var = 1). Rasch model fixes slope 1 leaves latent variance free, fix..1pl = TRUE 1PLM common slope fixed .val.1pl (latent variance fixed 1) rather usual Rasch identification. D = 1.702, slope logit scale D×=1.702D \times = 1.702. demonstrate approaches:

text: 3-parameter logistic model (3PLM) adds lower-asymptote (guessing) parameter gg 2PLM: P(Y=1∣θ)=g+(1−g)1+exp⁡(−D⋅⋅(θ−b)) P(Y = 1 \mid \theta) = g + \frac{(1 - g)}{1 + \exp(-D \cdot \cdot (\theta - b))} g∈[0,1)g \[0, 1) pseudo-guessing parameter, probability correct response even low ability levels. gg can poorly identified small samples (sometimes even large samples), two primary options handling gg est_irt(): Estimate gg Beta prior (use.gprior = TRUE): regularizes gg toward plausible range (e.g., 1/K1/K KK-option MC item), Fix gg constant value (fix.g = TRUE, g.val = ...): appropriate number response options known guessing assumed uniform. addition, priors discrimination (aa) difficulty (bb) can applied via use.aprior use.bprior. especially useful : item discrimination estimates may unstable Items extreme difficulty values (|b|>3|b| > 3) pull bb toward unreasonable values want incorporate substantive prior knowledge (e.g., discriminations typically follow log-normal distribution certain parameters)

title: Item Parameter Estimation
text: FAPC (Fixed Ability Parameter Calibration) treats examinee ability estimates known (fixed) constants estimates item parameters maximizing item-level likelihood conditional fixed abilities. approach widely used pretest item calibration, particularly stable group examinees already taken operational test (e.g., within CAT environment) proficiency estimates readily available. instance, CAT system, examinee encounters personalized sequence items: Operational items (scored): Used estimate update examinees’ abilities (θ\theta). Pretest items (interspersed unscored): Embedded within test accumulate response data; parameters unknown need calibrated. FAPC uses individual θ̂\hat{\theta} values obtained operational items calibrate pretest item independently. Compared FIPC, FAPC computationally much simpler. eliminates need EM iterations, item’s parameters can estimated single, straightforward optimization process. Consequently, calibration can begin immediately soon sufficient number responses accumulate specific pretest item.

title: Item Parameter Estimation
text: Given response uiju_{ij} examinee ii pretest item jj fixed ability estimate θ̂\hat{\theta}_i, item-level log-likelihood defined : ℓ(aj,bj)=∑=1Nlog⁡P(uij∣θ̂,aj,bj) \ell(a_j, b_j) = \sum_{=1}^{N} \log P(u_{ij} \mid \hat{\theta}_i,\, a_j,\, b_j) item parameters estimated directly maximizing log-likelihood expression via numerical optimization (e.g., using nlminb()). Unlike standard marginal maximum likelihood (MML) estimation FIPC, EM cycle involved θ\theta values treated fixed, observed data rather latent distribution integrated . priors used (example, use.gprior = TRUE 3PLM items, default), log prior densities added function, estimates Bayes modal; loglikelihood element -2loglikelihood printed summary() exclude log prior densities. Important Limitation: FAPC inherently treats estimated abilities θ̂\hat{\theta}_i true, error-free parameters (θi\theta_i), thereby ignoring ability estimation error (measurement error). omission can bias item parameter estimates, especially operational test relatively short θ̂\hat{\theta} estimates less precise. Additionally, prevent selection bias confounding calibration, random (non-adaptive) pretest administration design strongly preferred adaptive administration pretest items.

text: ✅ Simple: Direct MLE conditional θ̂\hat{\theta}, requiring complex latent distribution assumptions. ✅ Fast: EM iterations needed, making computationally trivial. ✅ Scalable: item calibrated independently; ideal large-scale item pools real-time distributed computing. ✅ Flexible: Compatible ability estimation method (MLE, EAP, MAP) derived operational test. ⚠️ Assumes θ\theta known without error: Treating θ̂\hat{\theta} fixed constant ignores measurement error. measurement error propagates calibration can bias item parameter estimates, especially operational form short. ⚠️ population distribution estimation: Unlike FIPC, FAPC estimate recover group-level latent trait distribution (μθ,σθ\mu_{\theta}, \sigma_{\theta}) abilities treated fixed data rather random effect.

previous_headings: Part 4: Multiple-Group Calibration with est_mg()
title: Item Parameter Estimation
text: many testing programs, different groups examinees take different test forms share common (anchor) items. Common scenarios include: Vertical scaling: Grades 3, 4, 5 take different form; common items link adjacent grades onto single developmental scale. Test form equating: Two alternate forms (Form Form B) share anchor items; goal place forms common score scale. International assessments: Different countries take translated/adapted forms; common items enable cross-national comparisons. Longitudinal studies: Different cohorts take evolving forms time; common items maintain scale continuity. Challenge: group may different ability distribution (e.g., Grade 3 examinees systematically less able Grade 5 examinees), simply pooling data across groups calibrating together confound item difficulty group ability. Solution: est_mg() simultaneously: Estimates item parameters Constrains anchor item parameters identical across groups Estimates group-specific ability distributions Places everything common scale

title: Item Parameter Estimation
text: est_mg() implements CINEG (Common-Item Non-Equivalent Groups) design. key features : Groups need take number items items overall. Common items can subset group’s form (just first last sections). Common item parameters automatically constrained equal across groups appear, mapped accurately matching item IDs. Group ability distributions freely estimated groups free.group. Without FIPC, least one group must left free.group reference group whose distribution fixes scale; otherwise est_mg() stops error. example, consider three groups sharing items follows: est_mg() automatically constrains parameters C1 items identical across Groups 1 2, C2 items identical across Groups 2 3. chain statistical constraints links three groups onto single, unified scale.
code: Group 1:  [Item A1 ... Common items (C1) ... Item A2 ...] Group 2:  [Item B1 ... Common items (C1, C2) ... Item B2 ...] Group 3:  [Item D1 ... Common items (C2) ... Item D2 ...]

Within summed-score group ss, expected proportion correct responses P̂(Xi=1∣Xs=s)\hat{P}(X_i = 1 \mid X_s = s) computed using Lord-Wingersky recursive algorithm (Lord & Wingersky, 1984), integrates IRF latent ability distribution without requiring individual θ̂\hat{\theta} estimates. text: irtQ provides run_mst() carry exactly kind simulation. Given item bank, route_map, module matrix, vector true abilities (pre-generated response matrix), run_mst() simulates full MST administration every examinee (stage--stage routing final scoring) returns resulting ability estimates together module pathway examinee traveled. examples use simMST 1-3-3 panel introduced : routing module Stage 1, followed three modules varying difficulty Stages 2 3. run_mst() supports three routing strategies. Two require fixed cut scores : default, route_method = "bmat", routes examinee reachable module whose mean item difficulty closest current ability estimate, route_method = "mfi" routes reachable module highest test information function (TIF) value current estimate. third, cut-score routing (route_method = NULL), compares current estimate fixed set cut scores. three, current estimate end stage computed responses modules examinee taken far, module just completed. Start default, bmat: closely related alternative maximum Fisher information (MFI) routing (route_method = "mfi"): instead comparing mean item difficulty, routes examinee reachable module provides highest TIF value current ability estimate. MFI routing assumes module’s TIF curve behaves intended, peaking higher harder modules theta increases, higher easier modules theta decreases. practice assumption can fail: harder module’s TIF curve may unexpectedly peak low theta value, low-ability examinees routed easy module instead get routed harder one. called anomalous routing, path reversal, opposite MST designed . Alternatively, setting route_method = NULL switches traditional cut-score routing (design commonly used operational MST programs), examinee’s intermediate ability estimate compared fixed set cut scores decide next module:

code: # Generate one response matrix from a fresh set of true abilities set.seed(123) theta_true2 <- rnorm(500, mean = 0, sd = 1) resp_matrix <- simdat(x = x, theta = theta_true2, D = 1.702) # resp_matrix is an N x J matrix (N examinees x J total items in the bank)  # bmat routing on the pre-generated responses result_A <- run_mst(   x            = x,   route_map    = route_map,   module       = module,   theta        = theta_true2,    # kept only for RMSE evaluation below   response     = resp_matrix,    # pre-generated N x J response matrix   D            = 1.702,   route_method = "bmat",   route_score  = list(method = "EAP", norm.prior = c(0, 1), nquad = 41),   final_score  = list(method = "ML", range = c(-4, 4)),   se           = FALSE )  # find_cut()-based cut-score routing on the SAME responses result_B <- run_mst(   x            = x,   route_map    = route_map,   module       = module,   theta        = theta_true2,   response     = resp_matrix,    # identical responses -> fair comparison   D            = 1.702,   route_method = NULL,   cut_score    = cut_result$cut_score,   route_score  = list(method = "EAP", norm.prior = c(0, 1), nquad = 41),   final_score  = list(method = "ML", range = c(-4, 4)),   se           = FALSE )  # Any RMSE difference now reflects the routing rule alone, not response noise rmse_A <- sqrt(mean((result_A$est.theta - theta_true2)^2)) rmse_B <- sqrt(mean((result_B$est.theta - theta_true2)^2)) cat(sprintf("RMSE (bmat):                 %.4f\n", rmse_A)) #> RMSE (bmat):                 0.3068 cat(sprintf("RMSE (find_cut cut scores):  %.4f\n", rmse_B)) #> RMSE (find_cut cut scores):  0.3050

Ideally, bias near zero across full ability range. Conditional Standard Error Measurement (CSEM): standard deviation ability estimates θ\theta level. Lower CSEM means precise measurement.

text: Conditional evaluation via simulation means repeating run_mst() procedure shown systematically across fixed grid ability levels, many replications grid point: Fix set true ability levels θ1,θ2,…\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots θk\theta_k, generate thousands simulated response patterns Route simulated examinee panel (exactly run_mst() ) using chosen routing rule (cut scores, b-matching, maximum information) Estimate ability simulated response compute mean variance estimates Bias = mean(θ̂\hat\theta) −-θk\theta_k, CSEM = Var(θ̂)\sqrt{\text{Var}(\hat\theta)} run_mst() already automates Steps 2-4 single θk\theta_k single batch replications; full evaluation just wraps loop ability grid sufficiently large number replications per grid point (Example 6 demonstrates exactly ). approach conceptually simple, looping run_mst() way inherits several practical drawbacks: Computationally inefficient: Thousands response patterns must generated scored Stochastic: Results fluctuate across simulation replications Time-consuming: Evaluating many panel designs cut score configurations requires many separate simulation runs

title: MST Panel Evaluation and Simulation
text: Lim et al. (2021) proposed fundamentally different approach: instead simulating individual examinees, method directly computes exact probability distribution every possible observed score every stage pathway using recursive algorithm. key insight conditional distribution observed sum score along pathway can built stage stage using Lord-Wingersky recursion (Lord & Wingersky, 1984). Given conditional score distribution modules visited far, joint distribution next stage can computed exactly, without random sampling. core logic recursion: Stage 1: Compute P(X1=x∣θ)P(X_1 = x \mid \theta) routing module using Lord-Wingersky recursion, X1X_1 total score Stage 1. Routing: possible score xx Stage 1, determine Stage 2 module test taker routed (using cut scores). converts score distribution pathway probability. Stage 2: Stage 2 pathway, compute joint distribution P(X1+X2=s∣θ,path)P(X_1 + X_2 = s \mid \theta, \text{path}) convolving Stage 1 score distribution conditional distribution assigned Stage 2 module. Continue recursively stages. Ability estimation: Convert possible final sum score θ̂\hat\theta estimate using inverse Test Characteristic Curve (TCC) method, method implied IRT-based summed scoring. Note linear interpolation (intpol): items non-zero guessing parameters (e.g., 3PLM), expected sum score never falls sum guessing parameters, θ̂\hat\theta exists observed scores less equal sum; θ̂\hat\theta exists maximum possible score either. intpol = TRUE (default), low scores mapped linear interpolation point (θmin,0)(\theta_{\min},\, 0) lowest TCC-reachable score point, maximum score receives θmax\theta_{\max} (two values range.tcc), every possible sum score receives ability estimate rather NA. Evaluate: Compute conditional mean variance θ̂\hat\theta given true θ\theta, derive conditional bias CSEM. method : Exact: probability distributions computed analytically, approximated random sampling Fast: Computation takes seconds, minutes hours Deterministic: Results reproducible without simulation noise General: panel design, cut score configuration, ability grid can evaluated single function call reval_mst() function irtQ implements recursion-based method, computing conditional bias CSEM Monte Carlo loop estimates simulation, analytically, single function call without simulation noise.

text: Plotting evaluation results provides intuitive picture panel’s measurement quality. Conditional bias (left) CSEM (right) simMST 1-3-3 panel across ability scale.
code: library(ggplot2)  # Plot the conditional bias and CSEM of an eval.tb table side by side, with a # reference line at zero bias and at the mean CSEM plot_bias_csem <- function(eval_tb, title = NULL) {   long <- rbind(     data.frame(theta = eval_tb$theta, value = eval_tb$bias, panel = "Conditional bias"),     data.frame(theta = eval_tb$theta, value = eval_tb$csem, panel = "CSEM")   )   # keep the bias panel on the left   long$panel <- factor(long$panel, levels = c("Conditional bias", "CSEM"))   ref <- data.frame(     panel = c("Conditional bias", "CSEM"),     value = c(0, mean(eval_tb$csem)),     line  = c("Zero bias", "Mean CSEM")   )   ref$panel <- factor(ref$panel, levels = levels(long$panel))   ggplot(long, aes(x = theta, y = value)) +     geom_hline(data = ref, aes(yintercept = value, linetype = line), colour = "red") +     geom_line(aes(colour = panel), linewidth = 0.8) +     geom_point(aes(colour = panel), size = 1.5) +     facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_y") +     # start every panel's y axis at zero or below     expand_limits(y = 0) +     scale_colour_manual(       values = c("Conditional bias" = "steelblue", "CSEM" = "darkorange"),       guide = "none"     ) +     scale_linetype_manual(       values = c("Zero bias" = "dashed", "Mean CSEM" = "dotted"),       breaks = c("Zero bias", "Mean CSEM")     ) +     labs(x = expression(theta), y = NULL, linetype = NULL, title = title) +     theme_bw() +     theme(legend.position = "bottom") }  eval_tb <- eval_result$eval.tb plot_bias_csem(eval_tb, title = "simMST 1-3-3 panel")

code: # Retrieve item metadata for the easiest and hardest complete pathways # (pathway 1 = low ability; last pathway = high ability) n_paths <- nrow(eval_result$panel.info$pathway)  meta_low  <- eval_result$item.by.path$stage.3$path.1          # low-ability path meta_high <- eval_result$item.by.path[[3]][[n_paths]]          # high-ability path  theta_grid <- seq(-4, 4, 0.1)  tif_low  <- info(x = meta_low,  theta = theta_grid, D = 1.702)$tif tif_high <- info(x = meta_high, theta = theta_grid, D = 1.702)$tif  # Stack the two curves and keep the pathways in this order in the legend path_labels <- c("Low-ability pathway (path 1)", "High-ability pathway (last path)") tif_df <- data.frame(   theta   = rep(theta_grid, 2),   tif     = c(tif_low, tif_high),   pathway = factor(rep(path_labels, each = length(theta_grid)), levels = path_labels) )  ggplot(tif_df, aes(x = theta, y = tif, colour = pathway, linetype = pathway)) +   geom_line(linewidth = 1) +   scale_colour_manual(values = c("steelblue", "darkorange")) +   scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed")) +   labs(     x = expression(theta), y = "Test information",     colour = NULL, linetype = NULL,     title = "Test information: low-ability vs. high-ability pathway"   ) +   theme_bw() +   theme(legend.position = "bottom")

text: 1-2-2 MST panel design. Stage 1, examinees begin module 1M. Stage 1, routed either 2E (easy) 2H (hard). Stage 2, can routed either 3E 3H regardless Stage 2 module took. Routing: Stage 1 → Stage 2: θ̂<0\hat\theta < 0 → M2 (Easy), θ̂≥0\hat\theta \geq 0 → M3 (Hard) Stage 2 → Stage 3: θ̂<0\hat\theta < 0 → M4 (Easy), θ̂≥0\hat\theta \geq 0 → M5 (Hard) gives 4 pathways: M1-M2-M4, M1-M2-M5, M1-M3-M4, M1-M3-M5.

what: Example 5: Comparing Two Cut Score Configurations
title: MST Panel Evaluation and Simulation
text: Cut score placement directly affects measurement bias. Placing cuts close centre can cause mid-ability examinees routed sub-optimally. compare simMST cut scores (-0.45 0.45) wider configuration c(-1.0, 1.0) 1-3-3 panel. Conditional bias CSEM comparison: simMST vs. wider cut scores 1-3-3 panel. panel, two configurations give almost conditional bias CSEM: largest difference 0.02 , large biases ability extremes . Wider cuts send examinees middle modules Stages 2 3, module paths differ, effect final precision small .
code: # Alternative cut scores: wider routing bands cut_score_wide <- list(c(-1.0, 1.0), c(-1.0, 1.0))  eval_wide <- reval_mst(   x         = x,   D         = 1.702,   route_map = route_map,   module    = module,   cut_score = cut_score_wide,   theta     = theta,   range.tcc = c(-7, 7) ) tb_orig <- eval_result$eval.tb tb_wide <- eval_wide$eval.tb  # Stack the bias and CSEM of both cut score configurations cut_labels <- c("simMST cuts (about -0.45 and 0.45)", "Wider cuts (-1.0 and 1.0)") cmp <- rbind(   data.frame(theta = tb_orig$theta, value = tb_orig$bias, panel = "Conditional bias", cuts = cut_labels[1]),   data.frame(theta = tb_wide$theta, value = tb_wide$bias, panel = "Conditional bias", cuts = cut_labels[2]),   data.frame(theta = tb_orig$theta, value = tb_orig$csem, panel = "CSEM", cuts = cut_labels[1]),   data.frame(theta = tb_wide$theta, value = tb_wide$csem, panel = "CSEM", cuts = cut_labels[2]) ) cmp$cuts <- factor(cmp$cuts, levels = cut_labels) # keep the bias panel on the left cmp$panel <- factor(cmp$panel, levels = c("Conditional bias", "CSEM"))  ggplot(cmp, aes(x = theta, y = value, colour = cuts, shape = cuts, linetype = cuts)) +   geom_hline(     data = data.frame(panel = factor("Conditional bias", levels = levels(cmp$panel)), value = 0),     aes(yintercept = value), colour = "grey50", linetype = "dotted"   ) +   geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +   geom_point(size = 1.8) +   facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_y") +   # start every panel's y axis at zero or below   expand_limits(y = 0) +   scale_colour_manual(values = c("steelblue", "darkorange")) +   scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 2)) +   scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed")) +   labs(     x = expression(theta), y = NULL,     colour = NULL, shape = NULL, linetype = NULL,     title = "simMST cut scores vs. wider cut scores"   ) +   theme_bw() +   theme(legend.position = "bottom") # Largest absolute differences between the two configurations max(abs(tb_wide$bias - tb_orig$bias)) #> [1] 0.02474664 max(abs(tb_wide$csem - tb_orig$csem)) #> [1] 0.01745606

Step 4: Confirm gap closes matched scoring. final check, re-run simulation route_score = list(method = "INV.TCC") final_score = list(method = "INV.TCC"), matching reval_mst()’s internal logic exactly: Comparing three tail grid points, EAP/ML condition diverged analytical curve: comparison, overlaid across full ability range: Empirical bias RMSE INV.TCC/INV.TCC run_mst() Monte Carlo simulation (points) overlaid analytical reval_mst() curve (line). table plot confirm conclusion: INV.TCC/INV.TCC condition tracks analytical bias RMSE closely across ability range, including extremes EAP/ML condition diverged.
code: # An explicit, independent evaluation grid theta_grid <- seq(-5, 5, 0.5) n_reps     <- 300   # simulated examinees per grid point  # Repeat each grid point n_reps times into one long vector of true abilities set.seed(2026) true_theta <- rep(theta_grid, each = n_reps) sim_mc <- run_mst(   x            = x,   route_map    = route_map,   module       = module,   theta        = true_theta,   D            = 1.702,   route_method = NULL,   cut_score    = cut_score,   route_score  = list(method = "EAP", norm.prior = c(0, 1), nquad = 41),   final_score  = list(method = "ML", range = c(-4, 4)),   se           = FALSE,   verbose      = FALSE )  # Empirical bias and RMSE at each grid point mc_tb <- data.frame(theta = true_theta, est.theta = sim_mc$est.theta) diff_mc  <- mc_tb$est.theta - mc_tb$theta bias_mc  <- tapply(diff_mc, mc_tb$theta, mean) rmse_mc  <- tapply(diff_mc, mc_tb$theta, function(d) sqrt(mean(d^2)))  mc_result <- data.frame(   theta = as.numeric(names(bias_mc)),   bias  = as.numeric(bias_mc),   rmse  = as.numeric(rmse_mc) ) mc_result <- mc_result[order(mc_result$theta), ] eval_grid <- reval_mst(   x         = x,   D         = 1.702,   route_map = route_map,   module    = module,   cut_score = cut_score,   theta     = theta_grid,   range.tcc = c(-7, 7) )  tb_grid      <- eval_grid$eval.tb tb_grid$rmse <- sqrt(tb_grid$sigma2 + tb_grid$bias^2) # Overlay the bias and RMSE of a run_mst() simulation (points) on the # analytical reval_mst() curves (lines) plot_mc_vs_analytical <- function(analytical, simulated, sim_label, sim_colour, title) {   ana_label <- "reval_mst() (analytical)"   ana <- rbind(     data.frame(theta = analytical$theta, value = analytical$bias, panel = "Bias"),     data.frame(theta = analytical$theta, value = analytical$rmse, panel = "RMSE")   )   sim <- rbind(     data.frame(theta = simulated$theta, value = simulated$bias, panel = "Bias"),     data.frame(theta = simulated$theta, value = simulated$rmse, panel = "RMSE")   ) title: Utility Functions
text: Beyond main analysis pipeline, irtQ includes set utility functions simulating item response data, computing information characteristic functions, supporting numerical integration ability scale, computing asymptotic standard errors item parameter estimates, scoring raw selected-response data 0/1 matrix suitable downstream analysis. Throughout vignette reuse two item metadata objects defined .
code: library(irtQ) set.seed(2026) # 15-item binary test (3PLM) meta_bin <- shape_df(   par.drm = list(     a = c(1.0, 1.2, 0.8, 1.4, 0.9, 1.1, 1.3, 0.7, 1.0, 1.2,           0.9, 1.1, 1.4, 0.85, 1.0),     b = c(-2.0, -1.5, -1.0, -0.5, -0.1, 0.2, 0.6, 0.9, 1.2, 1.6,           -0.8, -0.3,  0.5,  1.0, 1.8),     g = rep(0.15, 15)   ),   item.id = paste0("I", 1:15),   cats    = 2,   model   = "3PLM" )  # Mixed-format test: 5 dichotomous (3PLM) + 3 polytomous (GRM, 4 categories) meta_mix <- shape_df(   par.drm = list(     a = c(1.0, 1.2, 0.9, 1.1, 0.8),     b = c(-1.0, -0.3, 0.3, 0.8, 1.4),     g = rep(0.15, 5)   ),   par.prm = list(     a = c(1.5, 1.2, 1.0),     d = list(       c(-1.5, -0.2, 1.0),       c(-1.2,  0.1, 1.3),       c(-0.9,  0.4, 1.6)     )   ),   item.id = c(paste0("DRM", 1:5), paste0("GRM", 1:3)),   cats    = c(rep(2, 5), rep(4, 3)),   model   = c(rep("3PLM", 5), rep("GRM", 3)) )  # Common theta grid used by info(), traceline(), and lwrc() theta_grid <- seq(-4, 4, by = 0.1)

what: drm() and prm(): Item Response Probability Functions
title: Utility Functions
text: drm() prm() low-level probability functions behind traceline() (drm()), simdat() (prm()), internal likelihood estimation routines. compute item response probabilities directly IRT parameters useful whenever need category probabilities specific set theta values without constructing full item metadata frame.

previous_headings: drm() and prm(): Item Response Probability Functions
title: Utility Functions
text: drm() computes P(θ)P(\theta), probability correct response, one dichotomous items 1PLM, 2PLM, 3PLM: P(θ)=g+1−g1+exp⁡(−D⋅⋅(θ−b)), P(\theta) = g + \frac{1 - g}{1 + \exp(-D \cdot \cdot (\theta - b))},  aa discrimination, bb difficulty, gg guessing parameter (pseudo-chance level), DD scaling constant. Setting g=0g = 0 gives 2PLM; additionally fixing aa equal across items gives 1PLM. function returns matrix rows = theta values columns = items. useful check: 3PLM item, P(θ=b)=(1+g)/2P(\theta = b) = (1 + g)/2.

previous_headings: drm() and prm(): Item Response Probability Functions
title: Utility Functions
text: prm() computes category response probabilities single polytomous item GRM GPCM. returns matrix rows = theta values columns = score categories (0, 1, …, K−1K-1), rows always sum 1. d argument contains K−1K - 1 threshold parameters KK-category item: GRM: d holds K−1K - 1 difficulty thresholds bkb_k P(U≥k∣θ)=0.5P(U \geq k \mid \theta) = 0.5. categories ordered higher theta values yield higher expected scores. GPCM: d holds K−1K - 1 threshold parameters b1,…,bK−1b_1, \ldots, b_{K-1}, expressed item location minus step parameter category boundary. v=0v = 0 term model defined 0 internally (b0b_0 supplied), provide K−1K - 1 values. GRM GPCM use parameter names produce different probability profiles. GRM appropriate response categories ordered increasing difficulty thresholds; GPCM allows flexible step structures. PCM (special case GPCM slope 1), set = 1 D = 1.

what: info(): Item and Test Information Functions
title: Utility Functions
text: info() computes item information function (IIF) test information function (TIF) specified ability values. TIF sum IIFs reciprocal squared conditional standard error estimation: TIF(θ)=∑jIIFj(θ)=1/SE2(θ)\text{TIF}(\theta) = \sum_j \text{IIF}_j(\theta) = 1/\text{SE}^2(\theta). function returns object class "info" three components: $iif: matrix item information values (rows = items, columns = theta points), $tif: numeric vector TIF values theta point, $theta: theta grid supplied user. plot() method visualizes IIFs, TIF, conditional standard error estimation (CSEE = 1/TIF1/\sqrt{\text{TIF}}).

what: traceline(): Item and Test Characteristic Curves
title: Utility Functions
text: traceline() computes item characteristic curve (ICC), test characteristic curve (TCC), category response probabilities item specified ability grid. function returns object class "traceline" four components: $prob.cats: named list matrices, one per item, containing category response probabilities (columns resp.0, resp.1, …) theta value, $icc: matrix expected item scores (rows = theta, columns = items), $tcc: numeric vector expected total (summed) scores theta, $theta: theta grid supplied user. dichotomous items, ICC equals P(θ)P(\theta), probability correct response. polytomous items, ICC expected item score ∑kk⋅P(U=k∣θ)\sum_k k \cdot P(U = k \mid \theta). plot() method used visualization. Two key arguments control drawn: item.loc: item(s) plot; NULL plots TCC whole test. score.curve: FALSE (default) draws category response probability curves; TRUE draws expected item score curve (single curve per item). Note score.curve = FALSE overlap = FALSE, single item can specified item.loc (one panel per score category). plot multiple items simultaneously score.curve = FALSE, set overlap = TRUE (one panel per item, categories overlaid within panel).

title: Utility Functions
text: lwrc() implements Lord-Wingersky recursive algorithm (Kolen & Brennan, 2004; Lord & Wingersky, 1984), computes conditional distribution observed summed score given θ\theta: Pr⁡(X=s∣θ),s=0,1,…,∑j(Kj−1). \Pr(X = s \mid \theta), \quad s = 0, 1, \ldots, \sum_j (K_j - 1). distribution foundation IRT-based score equating used internally cac_lee(), reval_mst(), est_score() ("EAP.SUM" "INV.TCC" methods). tests polytomous items, algorithm generalizes straightforwardly ordered response categories. function supports two input modes: x argument (item metadata): computes conditional distribution specified theta value; returns matrix rows = summed scores (0,1,…,∑j(Kj−1)0, 1, \ldots, \sum_j (K_j - 1)) columns = theta levels. prob argument (x = NULL): user provides category probability matrix already evaluated particular theta, together cats vector; returns named vector summed-score probabilities. useful category probabilities come external source computing conditional distribution single fixed ability level.

title: Utility Functions
text: two results agree, confirming expected summed score derived lwrc() matches TCC value ability level.
code: # Conditional summed-score distribution at three ability levels lwrc_val <- lwrc(   x     = meta_bin,   theta = c(-1, 0, 1),   D     = 1.702 )  dim(lwrc_val)           # (J+1) rows x length(theta) columns: 16 x 3 #> [1] 16  3 round(head(lwrc_val), 4) #>         theta.1 theta.2 theta.3 #> score.0  0.0004  0.0000       0 #> score.1  0.0055  0.0000       0 #> score.2  0.0333  0.0001       0 #> score.3  0.1039  0.0012       0 #> score.4  0.1960  0.0087       0 #> score.5  0.2428  0.0377       0  # Verify: expected summed scores from lwrc() match the TCC from traceline() score_axis <- 0:(nrow(lwrc_val) - 1) colSums(lwrc_val * score_axis) #>   theta.1   theta.2   theta.3  #>  5.212989  8.137061 11.405212 # Cross-check with TCC from traceline() tcc_check <- traceline(x = meta_bin, theta = c(-1, 0, 1), D = 1.702)$tcc round(tcc_check, 6) #> [1]  5.212989  8.137061 11.405212

code: ## Example from Kolen & Brennan (2004, p. 183): 3 dichotomous items at a fixed theta # Each row is one item; columns are P(score=0) and P(score=1) probs_3items <- matrix(   c(0.26, 0.74,   # item 1: P(0) = 0.26, P(1) = 0.74     0.27, 0.73,   # item 2     0.18, 0.82),  # item 3   nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE ) cats_3items <- c(2, 2, 2)  score_dist <- lwrc(prob = probs_3items, cats = cats_3items) score_dist       # P(X=0), P(X=1), P(X=2), P(X=3) #>  score.0  score.1  score.2  score.3  #> 0.012636 0.127692 0.416708 0.442964 sum(score_dist)  # should equal 1 #> [1] 1 ## Mixed-format: 2 dichotomous + 1 four-category + 1 three-category item p1 <- c(0.3, 0.7, NA,  NA)    # dichotomous: 2 categories (cols: 0, 1) p2 <- c(0.4, 0.6, NA,  NA)    # dichotomous: 2 categories (cols: 0, 1) p3 <- c(0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.2)   # polytomous:  4 categories (cols: 0, 1, 2, 3) p4 <- c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2, NA)    # polytomous:  3 categories (cols: 0, 1, 2)  prob_mix <- rbind(p1, p2, p3, p4) cats_mix  <- c(2, 2, 4, 3)  score_dist_mix <- lwrc(prob = prob_mix, cats = cats_mix) score_dist_mix   # P(X=0) through P(X=7); max score = 1+1+3+2 = 7 #> score.0 score.1 score.2 score.3 score.4 score.5 score.6 score.7  #>  0.0060  0.0446  0.1410  0.2518  0.2758  0.1868  0.0772  0.0168 sum(score_dist_mix) #> [1] 1

title: Utility Functions
text: gen.weight() generates two-column data frame quadrature nodes normalized weights used numerical integration ability scale. used internally est_irt(), est_mg(), est_score(), sx2_fit(), covirt(), pcd2(), run_mst(), output can passed weights argument cac_lee() cac_rud(). Three distribution options available via dist argument: "norm": normal distribution. n given (theta), Gaussian quadrature points weights computed via statmod::gauss.quad.prob(). theta given, weights proportional normal density evaluated node. "unif": uniform distribution, equally spaced nodes [l,u][l, u] equal weights. "emp": empirical distribution, equal weights user-supplied theta values. returned data frame always columns named theta weight, weights always sum 1.
code: # 41 Gaussian quadrature points from N(0, 1), most common usage w_norm <- gen.weight(n = 41, dist = "norm", mu = 0, sigma = 1) head(w_norm) #>        theta       weight #> 1 -11.614937 2.257864e-30 #> 2 -10.647537 8.308559e-26 #> 3  -9.843433 2.746891e-22 #> 4  -9.123070 2.326384e-19 #> 5  -8.456099 7.655982e-17 #> 6  -7.826882 1.220335e-14 sum(w_norm$weight)      # always sums to 1 #> [1] 1  # Plot the quadrature approximation plot(w_norm$weight ~ w_norm$theta,      type = "h", lwd = 2,      xlab = expression(theta), ylab = "Weight",      main = "Gaussian Quadrature Approximation of N(0, 1) with 41 nodes") # Normal weights on a user-defined evenly spaced grid w_grid <- gen.weight(dist = "norm", mu = 0, sigma = 1,                      theta = seq(-4, 4, by = 0.25)) nrow(w_grid)   # 33 nodes #> [1] 33 sum(w_grid$weight) #> [1] 1 # Uniform distribution: 21 equally spaced nodes on [-3, 3] w_unif <- gen.weight(n = 21, dist = "unif", l = -3, u = 3) head(w_unif) #>   theta     weight #> 1  -3.0 0.04761905 #> 2  -2.7 0.04761905 #> 3  -2.4 0.04761905 #> 4  -2.1 0.04761905 #> 5  -1.8 0.04761905 #> 6  -1.5 0.04761905 # Empirical distribution: equal weights for sample ability estimates theta_sample <- rnorm(200) w_emp <- gen.weight(dist = "emp", theta = theta_sample) nrow(w_emp)              # one node per observation #> [1] 200 sum(w_emp$weight)        # sums to 1 #> [1] 1

what: covirt(): Asymptotic Variance-Covariance Matrices of Item Parameters
title: Utility Functions
text: covirt() computes analytical asymptotic variance-covariance matrices item parameter estimates expected information item, integrated assumed ability distribution (Li & Lissitz, 2004; Thissen & Wainer, 1982). matrices provide asymptotic standard errors (ASEs) maximum likelihood estimates without requiring examinee response data; item parameters, ability distribution, sample size used calibration needed. polytomous items, information multinomial response used, differs Equation A8 Li & Lissitz (2004); see ?covirt details. abilities treated known, model assumed fit, item parameter priors ignored, analytical ASEs generally considered lower bounds standard errors actual calibration (Li & Lissitz, 2004; Thissen & Wainer, 1982), best used approximations empirical standard errors calibration software unavailable. function returns named list two components: $cov: named list variance-covariance matrices, one per item, $se: named list ASE vectors (square roots diagonal elements covariance matrix). Notes PCM items: item metadata uses "GPCM" label Generalized Partial Credit Model (GPCM) Partial Credit Model (PCM). PCM items, whose slope estimated, must identified via pcm.loc argument; slope held value item metadata, thresholds enter variance-covariance matrix.

what: irtQ: Unidimensional Item Response Theory Modeling
title: irtQ: Unidimensional Item Response Theory Modeling
text: goal irtQ fit unidimensional item response theory (IRT) models data may include dichotomous polytomous items. package enables: Typical item parameter estimation Pretest item calibration Multiple-group item calibration Estimation examinees’ latent abilities Evaluation model-data fit item level Item parameter estimation conducted using marginal maximum likelihood estimation via expectation-maximization (MMLE-EM) algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981). pretest item calibration, irtQ supports: Fixed item parameter calibration (FIPC; Kim, 2006), Fixed ability parameter calibration (FAPC; Ban et al., 2001; Stocking, 1988). ability estimation, several widely used scoring methods available, including: Maximum likelihood estimation (ML) Maximum likelihood estimation fences (MLF; Han, 2016) Weighted likelihood estimation (WL; Warm, 1989) Maximum posteriori estimation (MAP; Hambleton et al., 1991) Expected posteriori estimation (EAP; Bock & Mislevy, 1982) EAP summed scoring (Thissen et al., 1995; Thissen & Orlando, 2001) Inverse test characteristic curve (TCC) scoring (e.g., Kolen & Brennan, 2004; Kolen & Tong, 2010; Stocking, 1996) Also, model fit assessment includes item fit statistics : Chi-square (X^2; Bock, 1960; Yen, 1981), Likelihood ratio chi-square (G^2; McKinley & Mills, 1985), Infit outfit statistics (Ames & Penfield, 2015) Graphical residual diagnostics (Hambleton et al., 1991) S-X^2 (Orlando & Thissen, 2000, 2003) addition, package offers variety utilities IRT analysis, including: Detecting differential item functioning (DIF) using RDIF, RDIF-CR (categorical residuals), GRDIF (multiple groups), CATSIB Detecting item parameter drift (IPD) using residual-based IPD (RIPD) framework pseudo-count D2 statistic Computing classification accuracy consistency indices Designing, evaluating, simulating multistage-adaptive test (MST) panels, including TIF-crossing cut-score selection, recursion-based analytical evaluation, Monte Carlo simulation full MST administrations Simulating response data Computing conditional distribution observed scores using Lord-Wingersky recursion Calculating item test information characteristic functions Visualizing item test characteristic information curves Importing item ability parameters popular IRT software (e.g., BILOG-MG, PARSCALE, flexMIRT, mirt R package; latter requires suggested mirt package), writing flexMIRT parameter files Running flexMIRT (Cai, 2017) R Windows Supporting additional tools flexible practical IRT analyses Beyond IRT-based analyses, package also provides small set classical test theory (CTT) functions (ctt(), freq_score(), ctt_distr(), score_resp()) computing traditional item- test-level statistics scoring selected-response item data. full documentation, including function references tutorial articles, visit package website: https://hwangQ.github.io/irtQ/. short introduction available vignette("irtQ", package = "irtQ").

what: 1. Item Calibration for a Linear Test Form
title: irtQ: Unidimensional Item Response Theory Modeling
text: Item parameter estimation linear test form can performed using irtQ::est_irt() function, implements marginal maximum likelihood estimation via expectation-maximization (MMLE-EM) algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981). function returns item parameter estimates along standard errors, computed cross-product approximation information matrix (Meilijson, 1989), information item parameter priors added. irtQ package supports calibration mixed-format tests containing dichotomous polytomous items. also provides flexible set options address various practical calibration needs. example, users can: Specify prior distributions item parameters Fix specific parameters (e.g., guessing parameter 3PL model) Estimate latent ability distribution using nonparametric histogram method (Woods, 2007) irtQ package, item calibration linear test form typically involves two main steps: Prepare examinees’ response data set linear test form estimate item parameters using irtQ::est_irt() function, response data set linear test form must first prepared. data provided either matrix data frame format, rows represent examinees columns represent items. missing responses, properly coded (e.g., NA). Estimate item parameters using irtQ::est_irt() function estimate item parameters, several key input arguments must specified irtQ::est_irt() function: data: matrix data frame containing examinees’ item responses. model: character vector specifying IRT model item (e.g., "1PLM", "2PLM", "3PLM", "GRM", "GPCM"). cats: numeric vector indicating number score categories item. dichotomous items, use 2. D: scaling constant; default, 1, gives logistic metric, 1.702 approximates normal ogive. Optionally, may incorporate prior distributions item parameters: use.aprior, use.bprior, use.gprior: Logical indicators specifying whether apply prior distributions discrimination (), difficulty (b), guessing (g) parameters, respectively. aprior, bprior, gprior: Lists specifying distributional form corresponding parameters prior. Supported distributions include Beta, Log-normal, Normal. missing responses coded value NA, specify value via missing argument. default, latent ability distribution assumed follow standard normal distribution (.e., N(0, 1)). However, users can estimate empirical histogram latent distribution setting EmpHist = TRUE, based nonparametric method proposed Woods (2007).

what: 2. Pretest Item Calibration with the Fixed Item Parameter Calibration (FIPC) Method (e.g., Kim, 2006)
title: irtQ: Unidimensional Item Response Theory Modeling
text: fixed item parameter calibration (FIPC) method widely used approach calibrating pretest items computerized adaptive testing (CAT). enables placement parameter estimates newly developed items onto scale operational item parameters (.e., scale item bank), without need post hoc linking rescaling procedures (Ban et al., 2001; Chen & Wang, 2016). FIPC, parameters operational items fixed, prior distribution latent ability variable estimated calibration process. estimated prior used place pretest item parameters scale fixed operational items (Kim, 2006). irtQ package, FIPC implemented following three steps: Prepare item metadata, including operational items (fixed) pretest items. perform FIPC using irtQ::est_irt() function, item metadata must first prepared. item metadata structured data frame includes essential information item, number score categories IRT model type. details, refer Details section irtQ::est_irt() documentation. FIPC procedure, metadata must contain : Operational items (whose parameters fixed), Pretest items (whose parameters freely estimated). pretest items, cats (number score categories) model (IRT model type) must accurately specified. However, item parameter values (e.g., par.1, par.2, par.3) metadata serve placeholders can arbitrary, since actual parameter estimates obtained calibration. facilitate creation metadata FIPC, helper function irtQ::shape_df_fipc() can used. Prepare response data set examinees answered operational pretest items. implement FIPC using irtQ::est_irt() function, examinees’ response data test form must provided, including operational pretest items. response data matrix data frame format, rows represent examinees columns represent items. Note column order response data must exactly match row order item metadata. Perform FIPC using irtQ::est_irt() function calibrate pretest items. FIPC performed using irtQ::est_irt() function, parameters pretest items estimated parameters operational items fixed. implement FIPC, must provide following arguments irtQ::est_irt(): x: item metadata, including operational pretest items. data: examinee response data corresponding item metadata. fipc = TRUE: Enables fixed item parameter calibration. fipc.method: Specifies FIPC method used (e.g., "MEM"). fix.loc: vector indicating positions operational items fixed. Optionally, may estimate empirical histogram scale latent ability distribution setting EmpHist = TRUE. EmpHist = FALSE, normal prior assumed scale updated iteratively EM algorithm. additional details implementing FIPC, refer documentation irtQ::est_irt().

what: 3. Pretest Item Calibration with the Fixed Ability Parameter Calibration (FAPC) Method (e.g., Stocking, 1988)
title: irtQ: Unidimensional Item Response Theory Modeling
text: computerized adaptive testing (CAT), fixed ability parameter calibration (FAPC) method, also known Stocking’s Method (Stocking, 1988), one simplest straightforward approaches calibrating pretest items. involves estimating item parameters using maximum likelihood (Bayes modal estimation prior distributions used), conditional known estimated proficiency values. FAPC primarily used place parameter estimates pretest items onto scale operational item parameters. can also used recalibrate operational items evaluating potential item parameter drift (Chen & Wang, 2016; Stocking, 1988). typically applied pretest items, often administered randomly rather adaptively (Ban et al., 2001; Chen & Wang, 2016). irtQ package, FAPC can conducted two main steps: Prepare data set containing item response data corresponding ability (proficiency) estimates. use irtQ::est_item() function, two input data sets required: Ability estimates: numeric vector containing examinees’ ability (proficiency) estimates. Item response data: matrix data frame containing item responses, rows represent examinees columns represent items. order examinees response data must exactly match order ability estimates. Estimate item parameters using irtQ::est_item() function. irtQ::est_item() function estimates pretest item parameters based provided ability estimates. use function, must specify following arguments (x, item metadata data frame, place model cats): data: matrix data frame containing examinees’ item responses. score: numeric vector examinees’ ability (proficiency) estimates. model: character vector specifying IRT model item (e.g., "1PLM", "2PLM", "3PLM", "GRM", "GPCM"). cats: numeric vector indicating number score categories item. dichotomous items, use 2. D: scaling constant; default, 1, gives logistic metric, 1.702 approximates normal ogive. additional details implementing FAPC, refer documentation irtQ::est_item().

Two options available: "average": Uses average ability estimate within group "middle": Uses midpoint interval implement step, specify item metadata (x), ability estimates (score), response data (data) arguments irtQ::irtfit() function. want use fewer ten ability groups, adjust n.width argument accordingly. response data contain missing values, specify missing value code using missing argument. code: ## Example: Find the theta value corresponding to a given probability ## of a correct response using the item response function of a 2PLM ## (a = 1, b = 0.2)  # Define a function of theta find.th <- function(theta, p) {   p - drm(theta = theta, a = 1, b = 0.2, D = 1) }  # Find the theta value corresponding to p = 0.2 bisection(.fun = find.th, p = 0.2, lb = -10, ub = 10)$root #> [1] -1.186256  # Find the theta value corresponding to p = 0.8 bisection(.fun = find.th, p = 0.8, lb = -10, ub = 10)$root #> [1] 1.586266

title: Classification Accuracy and Consistency Using Lee's (2010) Approach — cac_lee
text: x data frame containing item metadata (e.g., item parameters, number categories, IRT model types, etc.). See est_irt() simdat() details item metadata. data frame can easily created using shape_df() function. cutscore numeric vector finite cut scores strictly ascending order. K - 1 cut scores divide examinees K performance levels. cut.obs = TRUE, cut scores observed summed score metric. cut.obs = FALSE, ability (theta) metric. score equal cut score assigned higher level. theta numeric vector ability estimates, one per examinee, used P method. ignored weights supplied. Missing values (NA) excluded warning. code: # \donttest{ # Load required package library("dplyr") #>  #> Attaching package: ‘dplyr’ #> The following objects are masked from ‘package:stats’: #>  #>     filter, lag #> The following objects are masked from ‘package:base’: #>  #>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union  ## Uniform DIF Detection ############################################### # (1) Simulate data with true uniform DIF ###############################################  # Import the "-prm.txt" output file from flexMIRT flex_sam <- system.file("extdata", "flexmirt_sample-prm.txt", package = "irtQ")  # Select 36 3PLM items that are non-DIF par_nstd <-   bring.flexmirt(file = flex_sam, "par")$Group1$full_df %>%   dplyr::filter(.data$model == "3PLM") %>%   dplyr::filter(dplyr::row_number() %in% 1:36) %>%   dplyr::select(1:6) par_nstd$id <- paste0("nondif", 1:36)  # Generate four new items to contain uniform DIF difpar_ref <-   shape_df(     par.drm = list(a = c(0.8, 1.5, 0.8, 1.5), b = c(0.0, 0.0, -0.5, -0.5), g = rep(0.15, 4)),     item.id = paste0("dif", 1:4), cats = 2, model = "3PLM"   )  # Introduce uniform DIF in the focal group by shifting b-parameters difpar_foc <-   difpar_ref %>%   dplyr::mutate_at(.vars = "par.2", .funs = function(x) x + rep(0.7, 4))  # Combine the 4 DIF and 36 non-DIF items for both reference and focal groups # Therefore, the first four items now exhibit uniform DIF par_ref <- rbind(difpar_ref, par_nstd) par_foc <- rbind(difpar_foc, par_nstd)  # Generate true theta values set.seed(123) theta_ref <- rnorm(500, 0.0, 1.0) theta_foc <- rnorm(500, 0.0, 1.0)  # Simulate response data resp_ref <- simdat(par_ref, theta = theta_ref, D = 1) resp_foc <- simdat(par_foc, theta = theta_foc, D = 1) data <- rbind(resp_ref, resp_foc)  ############################################### # text: According Penfield (2010), differential item functioning (DIF) polytomously scored items can conceptualized two forms: global DIF net DIF. Global DIF refers differences groups conditional probabilities responding specific score categories, thus offering fine-grained view DIF category level. contrast, net DIF summarizes differences single value representing overall impact DIF item's expected score. RDIF framework using categorical residuals (RDIF-CR), implemented crdif(), extends original residual-based DIF framework proposed Lim et al. (2022) detect global DIF polytomous items (Jung & Lim, 2026; Lim, Malatesta, & Lee, 2024). framework includes three statistics: \(RDIF_{R}-CR\), \(RDIF_{S}-CR\), \(RDIF_{RS}-CR\), designed capture different aspects group-level differences categorical response patterns. illustrate RDIF-CR framework operates, consider item five ordered score categories (\(k \\{0,1,2,3,4\}\)). Suppose examinee latent ability \(\theta\) responds category 2. one-hot encoded response vector response \((0,0,1,0,0)^T\). Assume IRT model predicts category probabilities \((0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.25, 0.05)^T\), expected item score \(0(0.1) + 1(0.2) + 2(0.4) + 3(0.25) + 4(0.05) = 1.95\). RDIF-CR framework, categorical residual vector calculated subtracting predicted probability vector one-hot response vector, resulting \((-0.1, -0.2, 0.6, -0.25, -0.05)^T\). contrast, net DIF assessed single item score residual, observed item score minus expected item score. example, residual \(2 - 1.95 = 0.05\). detect net DIF, use rdif(). \(RDIF_{R}-CR\) quadratic form vector category-level differences mean raw residuals focal reference groups, centered null mean, generalized inverse null covariance matrix. \(RDIF_{S}-CR\) corresponding statistic mean squared residuals, \(RDIF_{RS}-CR\) uses two vectors combined. null hypothesis DIF, statistic asymptotically follows chi-square distribution whose degrees freedom equal rank covariance matrix (Moore, 1977). item K score categories (K 3 ), K category residuals examinee sum zero, elements \(RDIF_{R}-CR\) vector also sum zero covariance matrix rank K - 1. \(RDIF_{R}-CR\) therefore K - 1 degrees freedom. computed dropping one score category, gives value Moore-Penrose generalized inverse full covariance matrix, category dropped raw residual part \(RDIF_{RS}-CR\). squared residuals subject constraint holds examinees, \(RDIF_{S}-CR\) K degrees freedom, \(RDIF_{RS}-CR\) 2K - 1. dichotomous item, two category residuals negatives , residual score category 1 used, three statistics 1, 1, 2 degrees freedom; title: Item parameter estimation using MMLE-EM algorithm — est_irt
text: function fits unidimensional item response theory (IRT) models mixed-format data comprising dichotomous polytomous items, using marginal maximum likelihood estimation via expectation-maximization (MMLE-EM) algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981). prior distributions specified item parameters, estimates modes marginal posterior distribution (Bayes modal estimates). function also supports fixed item parameter calibration (FIPC; Kim, 2006), practical method pretest (newly developed) item calibration computerized adaptive testing (CAT). FIPC enables parameter estimates pretest items placed scale operational items (Ban et al., 2001). dichotomous items, function supports one-, two-, three-parameter logistic models. polytomous items, supports graded response model (GRM) (generalized) partial credit model (GPCM).

title: Fixed ability parameter calibration — est_item
text: function performs fixed ability parameter calibration (FAPC), often called Stocking's (1988) Method , estimates item parameters maximum likelihood given ability estimates (Baker & Kim, 2004; Ban et al., 2001; Stocking, 1988). prior distributions specified item parameters (default, guessing parameters 3PLM items), estimates modes posterior distribution (Bayes modal estimates). can also considered special case joint maximum likelihood estimation one cycle item parameter estimation conducted, conditioned given ability estimates (Birnbaum, 1968). FAPC potentially useful method calibrating pretest (newly developed) items computerized adaptive testing (CAT), enables placing parameter estimates scale operational items. addition, can used recalibrate operational items item bank evaluate potential parameter drift (Chen & Wang, 2016; Stocking, 1988).

title: Multiple-group item calibration using MMLE-EM algorithm — est_mg
text: function performs multiple-group item calibration (Bock & Zimowski, 1997) using marginal maximum likelihood estimation via expectation-maximization (MMLE-EM) algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981). prior distributions specified item parameters, estimates modes marginal posterior distribution (Bayes modal estimates). also supports multiple-group fixed item parameter calibration (MG-FIPC; e.g., Kim & Kolen, 2016), extends single-group FIPC method (Kim, 2006) multiple-group settings. dichotomous items, function supports one-, two-, three-parameter logistic IRT models. polytomous items, graded response model (GRM) (generalized) partial credit model (GPCM) available.

title: Estimate examinees' ability (proficiency) parameters — est_score
text: function estimates examinees' latent ability parameters. Available scoring methods include maximum likelihood estimation (ML), maximum likelihood estimation fences (MLF; Han, 2016), weighted likelihood estimation (WL; Warm, 1989), maximum posteriori estimation (MAP; Hambleton et al., 1991), expected posteriori estimation (EAP; Bock & Mislevy, 1982), EAP summed scoring (Thissen et al., 1995; Thissen & Orlando, 2001), inverse test characteristic curve (TCC) scoring (e.g., Kolen & Brennan, 2004; Kolen & Tong, 2010; Stocking, 1996).

title: Find TIF-Crossing Cut Scores for MST Routing — find_cut
text: run_mst uses Maximum Fisher Information (MFI) routing (route_method = "mfi"), selects next-stage module maximizes TIF examinee's current ability estimate. principle, harder module always higher TIF high-ability examinees, lower TIF low-ability examinees, making MFI routing work intended. However, practice, harder module's TIF curve can peak theta value unexpectedly low, harder module also highest TIF near low end ability scale. case, low-ability examinee incorrectly routed harder module, opposite MST designed . called anomalous routing path reversal.

title: Find TIF-Crossing Cut Scores for MST Routing — find_cut
text: find_cut() resolves problem computing cut scores TIF curves , rather relying pure MFI time routing. Specifically, pair modules adjacent module index (follow order difficulty; see Module index vs. difficulty order), function finds theta value higher-index module's TIF first overtakes lower-index module's TIF theta increases. crossing point natural boundary two modules: , lower-index (easier) module informative; , higher-index (harder) module informative. Using point fixed cut score pre-empts path reversals MFI routing produces extremes scale.

title: Find TIF-Crossing Cut Scores for MST Routing — find_cut
text: Two TIF curves may cross . find_cut() distinguishes two types crossing: Proper crossing: difference \(\text{TIF}_{\text{right}}(\theta) - \text{TIF}_{\text{left}}(\theta)\), right module higher-index (intended harder) module pair, changes sign negative positive (positive slope crossing). correct, expected crossing middle theta scale. Anomalous crossing: difference changes sign positive negative (negative slope crossing). corresponds pathological situation harder module temporarily dominates low end theta scale, pattern causes path reversals MFI routing. proper crossings used cut scores. Anomalous crossings reported $details diagnostic purposes excluded returned cut_score. proper crossing found module pair, informative error thrown. multiple proper crossings found (unusual well-designed modules), warning issued one closest ref_theta selected.

title: Find TIF-Crossing Cut Scores for MST Routing — find_cut
code: ## Setup: use the built-in simMST 1-3-3 panel ## simMST is a 7-module, 3-stage MST panel (8 dichotomous 3PLM items each). ## Modules 1 (routing), 2-4 (stage 2: easy/medium/hard), ##         5-7 (stage 3: easy/medium/hard). x         <- simMST$item_bank module    <- simMST$module route_map <- simMST$route_map  ## Find TIF-crossing cut scores ## For each adjacent module pair at stages 2 and 3, find_cut() identifies ## the theta at which the harder module's TIF first exceeds the easier ## module's TIF (proper crossing), and returns it as a cut score. cut_result <- find_cut(x = x, module = module, route_map = route_map, D = 1.702)  ## Print a summary: crossing points found, anomalous crossings excluded, ## and the final selected cut scores per stage transition. print(cut_result) #> MST TIF-Crossing Cut Score Results #> ================================================== #>  #> stage.2 #> ----------------------------------- #>   Modules (index order)    : 2, 3, 4 #>   Modules (difficulty order): 2, 3, 4 #>   Mean item locations      : -0.87, -0.0574, 0.7858 #>   Selected cut score(s)    : -0.4451, 0.4589 #>   Pair details: #>     [mod2_vs_mod3] #>       Proper crossing(s)    : 1  [theta = -0.4451] #>       Anomalous crossing(s) : 1  [theta = 3.3893]  (excluded) #>       Selected cut score    : -0.4451 #>     [mod3_vs_mod4] #>       Proper crossing(s)    : 1  [theta = 0.4589] #>       Selected cut score    : 0.4589 #>  #> stage.3 #> ----------------------------------- #>   Modules (index order)    : 5, 6, 7 #>   Modules (difficulty order): 5, 6, 7 #>   Mean item locations      : -0.5586, -0.042, 0.5066 #>   Selected cut score(s)    : -0.4171, 0.4532 #>   Pair details: #>     [mod5_vs_mod6] #>       Proper crossing(s)    : 1  [theta = -0.4171] #>       Anomalous crossing(s) : 1  [theta = 1.617]  (excluded) #>       Selected cut score    : -0.4171 #>     [mod6_vs_mod7] #>       Proper crossing(s)    : 1  [theta = 0.4532] #>       Anomalous crossing(s) : 1  [theta = -1.9874]  (excluded) #>       Selected cut score    : 0.4532 #> ================================================== #> Usage: run_mst(..., route_method = NULL, cut_score = <result>$cut_score)  ## Visualize TIF curves and cut scores ## plot() shows TIF curves for every module faceted by stage. ## Selected cut scores appear as solid black vertical lines with theta ## labels at the crossing point. Anomalous crossings (if any) appear ## as dashed red lines. plot(cut_result)                         # stages stacked vertically (default)  plot(cut_result, layout = "horizontal")  # stages side by side  plot(cut_result, show_anomalous = FALSE) # hide anomalous crossing markers   ## Inspect the cut_score element, a list that can be passed to run_mst() ## cut_score[[1]]: two cut scores for the stage-1 -> stage-2 transition ## cut_score[[2]]: cut scores for the stage-2 -> stage-3 transition cut_result$cut_score #> $stage.2 #> [1] -0.4450901  0.4588774 #>  #> $stage.3 #> [1] -0.4170988  0.4531584 #>   ## Compare with the cut scores stored in simMST, which were obtained the ## same way; the two sets agree up to numerical precision simMST$cut_score #> $stage.2 #> [1] -0.4450901  0.4588774 #>  #> $stage.3 #> [1] -0.4170988  0.4531584 #>  all.equal(cut_result$cut_score, simMST$cut_score) #> [1] TRUE  ## Use the cut scores in run_mst() ## Pass cut_result$cut_score directly to run_mst() with route_method = NULL. ## This replaces pure MFI routing with TIF-crossing-based fixed cut scores, ## preventing anomalous path reversals at the extremes of the theta scale. # \donttest{ set.seed(1) theta_true <- rnorm(500) result <- run_mst(   x            = x,   route_map    = route_map,   module       = module,   theta        = theta_true,   D            = 1.702,   route_method = NULL,   cut_score    = cut_result$cut_score,   verbose      = FALSE ) # }

title: irtQ: Unidimensional Item Response Theory Modeling — irtQ-package
text: irtQ package provides tools fitting unidimensional item response theory (IRT) models test data include dichotomous polytomous items. enables calibration pretest item parameters, estimation examinees' abilities, offers comprehensive suite utilities unidimensional IRT analysis, including model-data fit evaluation, differential item functioning (DIF) detection, . item parameter estimation, package employs marginal maximum likelihood estimation via expectation-maximization (MMLE-EM) algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981). calibrate pretest (newly developed) items, supports fixed item parameter calibration (FIPC; Kim, 2006) fixed ability parameter calibration (FAPC; Ban et al., 2001; Stocking, 1988), also known Stocking's Method . addition, package offers multiple-group item calibration via MMLE-EM algorithm (est_mg(); Bock & Zimowski, 1997). ability estimation, several widely used scoring methods available, including: Maximum likelihood estimation (ML) Maximum likelihood estimation fences (MLF; Han, 2016) Weighted likelihood estimation (WL; Warm, 1989) Maximum posteriori estimation (MAP; Hambleton et al., 1991) Expected posteriori estimation (EAP; Bock & Mislevy, 1982) EAP summed scoring (Thissen et al., 1995; Thissen & Orlando, 2001) Inverse test characteristic curve (TCC) scoring (e.g., Kolen & Brennan, 2004; Kolen & Tong, 2010; Stocking, 1996) addition, package offers variety utilities IRT analysis, including: Evaluating model-data fit item fit statistics (irtfit(), sx2_fit()) Detecting DIF RDIF, RDIF-CR, GRDIF (multiple groups), CATSIB (rdif(), crdif(), grdif(), catsib()) Detecting item parameter drift (IPD) residual-based RIPD framework pseudo-count D2 statistic (ripd(), pcd2()) Computing classification accuracy consistency indices (cac_lee(), cac_rud()) Evaluating simulating multistage-adaptive test (MST) panels (panel_info(), reval_mst(), run_mst(), find_cut()) Importing item ability parameters BILOG-MG, PARSCALE, flexMIRT, mirt package (bring.flexmirt()), writing flexMIRT parameter files (write.flexmirt()) Running flexMIRT (Cai, 2017) R Windows (run_flexmirt()) Simulating response data Computing conditional distribution observed scores using Lord-Wingersky recursion Calculating item test information characteristic functions Visualizing item test characteristic information curves Beyond IRT-based analyses, package also provides small set classical test theory (CTT) functions (ctt(), freq_score(), ctt_distr(), score_resp()) computing traditional item- test-level statistics scoring selected-response item data.
