title: irtQ: Unidimensional Item Response Theory Modeling — irtQ-package
text: irtQ package supports dichotomous polytomous item response theory (IRT) models. dichotomous items, one-, two-, three-parameter logistic models (1PLM, 2PLM, 3PLM) available. polytomous items, graded response model (GRM) (generalized) partial credit model (GPCM) implemented. fitting partial credit model (PCM), note item discrimination (slope) parameters fixed 1. following, let \(Y\) response examinee latent ability \(\theta\) item, suppose polytomous item \(K\) unique score categories. IRT 1-3PL models IRT 1PLM, 2PLM, 3PLM models, probability examinee ability \(\theta\) responds correctly item given : $$P(Y = 1 \mid \theta) =       g + \frac{(1 - g)}{1 + \exp(-Da(\theta - b))},$$ \(\) item discrimination (slope) parameter, \(b\) item difficulty parameter, \(g\) guessing parameter. constant \(D\) scaling factor. \(D = 1\) (default irtQ), model logistic metric; \(D = 1.702\) makes logistic function approximate normal ogive function. 1PLM used, discrimination parameter \(\) either fixed constant value (e.g., \(= 1\)) constrained equal across items. 1PLM 2PLM models, guessing parameter fixed \(g = 0\). GRM graded response model (GRM), probability examinee latent ability \(\theta\) responds score category \(k\) (\(k = 0, 1, \ldots, K - 1\)) given : $$P(Y = k \mid \theta) = P^{*}(Y \ge k \mid \theta) - P^{*}(Y \ge k + 1 \mid \theta),$$ $$P^{*}(Y \ge k \mid \theta) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-Da(\theta - b_{k}))},$$ $$P^{*}(Y \ge k + 1 \mid \theta) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-Da(\theta - b_{k+1}))},$$ \(P^{*}(Y \ge k \mid \theta)\) cumulative probability (category boundary function) score category \(k\), functional form similar 2PL model. parameter \(b_{k}\) represents difficulty (threshold) parameter associated boundary categories \(k - 1\) \(k\). Note probability responding lowest highest score category can written : $$P(Y = 0 \mid \theta) = 1 - P^{*}(Y \ge 1 \mid \theta),$$ $$P(Y = K - 1 \mid \theta) = P^{*}(Y \ge K - 1 \mid \theta).$$ GPCM generalized partial credit model (GPCM), probability examinee latent ability \(\theta\) responds score category \(k\) (\(k = 0, 1, \ldots, K - 1\)) given : $$       P(Y = k \mid \theta) =       \frac{\exp\left(\sum_{v = 0}^{k} Da(\theta - b_v)\right)}       {\sum_{h = 0}^{K - 1} \exp\left(\sum_{v = 0}^{h} Da(\theta - b_v)\right)},     $$ \(b_v\) threshold (step) parameter associated category boundary \(v\) item. alternative parameterizations, \(b_v\) can expressed \(b_v = \beta - \tau_v\), \(\beta\) overall location (difficulty) parameter item, \(\tau_v\) threshold score category \(v\). irtQ package, item \(K\) unique score categories requires \(K - 1\) threshold parameters. \(v = 0\) term sums defined 0 (\(b_0\) free parameter), numerator lowest category \(\exp(0) = 1\). fitting partial credit model, item discrimination parameter \(\) fixed 1. GRM GPCM item \(K = 2\) score categories equivalent 2PLM item. item metadata one threshold par.2 NA par.3, info() traceline() compute values 2PLM.

title: irtQ: Unidimensional Item Response Theory Modeling — irtQ-package
text: Item parameter estimation linear test form can performed using est_irt() function, implements marginal maximum likelihood estimation via expectation-maximization (MMLE-EM) algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981). function returns item parameter estimates along standard errors, computed cross-product approximation information matrix (Meilijson, 1989), information item parameter priors added. irtQ package supports calibration mixed-format tests containing dichotomous polytomous items. also provides flexible set options address various practical calibration needs. example, users can: Specify prior distributions item parameters Fix specific parameters (e.g., guessing parameter 3PL model) Estimate latent ability distribution using nonparametric histogram method (Woods, 2007) irtQ package, item calibration linear test form typically involves two main steps: Prepare examinees' response data set linear test form estimate item parameters using est_irt() function, response data set linear test form must first prepared. data provided either matrix data frame format, rows represent examinees columns represent items. missing responses, properly coded (e.g., NA). Estimate item parameters using est_irt() function estimate item parameters, several key input arguments must specified est_irt() function: data: matrix data frame containing examinees' item responses. model: character vector specifying IRT model item (e.g., "1PLM", "2PLM", "3PLM", "GRM", "GPCM"). cats: numeric vector indicating number score categories item. dichotomous items, use 2. D: scaling constant. Use default D = 1 logistic metric, D = 1.702 approximate normal ogive model. Optionally, may incorporate prior distributions item parameters: use.aprior, use.bprior, use.gprior: Logical indicators specifying whether apply prior distributions discrimination (), difficulty (b), guessing (g) parameters, respectively. aprior, bprior, gprior: Lists specifying distributional form corresponding parameters prior. Supported distributions include Beta, Log-normal, Normal. Missing responses coded NA need setting; another code used (e.g., -9), give missing argument. default, latent ability distribution assumed follow standard normal distribution (.e., N(0, 1)). However, users can estimate empirical histogram latent distribution setting EmpHist = TRUE, based nonparametric method proposed Woods (2007).

title: irtQ: Unidimensional Item Response Theory Modeling — irtQ-package
text: computerized adaptive testing (CAT), fixed ability parameter calibration (FAPC) method (also known Stocking's Method ; Stocking, 1988) one simplest straightforward approaches calibrating pretest items. involves estimating item parameters using maximum likelihood estimation, conditional known estimated proficiency values. FAPC primarily used place parameter estimates pretest items onto scale operational item parameters. can also used recalibrate operational items evaluating potential item parameter drift (Chen & Wang, 2016; Stocking, 1988). method known produce accurate unbiased item parameter estimates items randomly administered examinees, rather adaptively, often case pretest items (Ban et al., 2001; Chen & Wang, 2016). irtQ package, FAPC can conducted two main steps: Prepare data set containing item response data corresponding ability (proficiency) estimates. use est_item() function, two input data sets required: Ability estimates: numeric vector containing examinees' ability (proficiency) estimates. Item response data: matrix data frame containing item responses, rows represent examinees columns represent items. order examinees response data must exactly match order ability estimates. Estimate item parameters using est_item() function. est_item() function estimates pretest item parameters based provided ability estimates. use function, must specify following arguments: data: matrix data frame containing examinees' item responses. score: numeric vector examinees' ability (proficiency) estimates. model: character vector specifying IRT model item (e.g., "1PLM", "2PLM", "3PLM", "GRM", "GPCM"). cats: numeric vector indicating number score categories item. dichotomous items, use 2. D: scaling constant. Use default D = 1 logistic metric, D = 1.702 approximate normal ogive model. additional details implementing FAPC, refer documentation est_item().

title: irtQ: Unidimensional Item Response Theory Modeling — irtQ-package
text: examples demonstrate estimate item parameters linear test form, calibrate pretest items using FIPC FAPC methods. examples use simulated data sets, examinees' response data generated based true item parameters true ability values using simdat() function. examples utilize item parameter estimates imported flexMIRT output file sample, includes mixed-format test 55 items: 50 dichotomous items modeled 3PLM 5 polytomous items modeled GRM. item parameters treated "true" values data generation. Specifically: Items 1-38: 3PLM items Items 39-40: GRM items Items 41-52: 3PLM items Items 53-55: GRM items (5 score categories) Example 1: Estimating item parameters linear test form example uses first 40 items (38 3PLM 2 GRM) form linear test. test assumed administered reference group 2,000 examinees whose latent ability follows standard normal distribution, N(0, 1). Examples 2 3: Calibrating pretest items using FIPC FAPC examples assume new test form consisting 55 items described . first 40 items treated fixed operational items (.e., Example 1), remaining 15 items newly developed pretest items calibrated. new test form administered separate group 2,000 examinees, whose ability distribution assumed follow \(N(0.5, 1.3^2)\). calibration pretest items conducted scale old form using FIPC FAPC procedures, respectively.
code: # Attach the packages library(irtQ)  ##--------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## 1. Item parameter estimation for a linear test form ##---------------------------------------------------------------------------  ## Step 1: Prepare response data for the reference group ## Import the "-prm.txt" output file from flexMIRT meta_true <- system.file("extdata", "flexmirt_sample-prm.txt", package = "irtQ")  # Extract item metadata using `irtQ::bring.flexmirt()` # This will serve as the base test form for later pretest item examples x_new <- irtQ::bring.flexmirt(file = meta_true, "par")$Group1$full_df  # Extract items 1 to 40 to define the linear test form used in this illustration x_ref <- x_new[1:40, ]  # Generate true ability values (N = 2,000) from N(0, 1) for the reference group set.seed(20) theta_ref <- rnorm(2000, mean = 0, sd = 1)  # Simulate response data for the linear test form # Scaling factor D = 1 assumes a logistic IRT model data_ref <- irtQ::simdat(x = x_ref, theta = theta_ref, D = 1)  ## Step 2: Estimate item parameters for the linear test form mod_ref <- irtQ::est_irt(   data       = data_ref,                              # Response data   D          = 1,                                     # Scaling factor   model      = c(rep("3PLM", 38), rep("GRM", 2)),     # Item models   cats       = c(rep(2, 38), rep(5, 2)),              # Score categories per item   item.id    = paste0("Ref_I", 1:40),                 # Item IDs   use.gprior = TRUE,                                  # Use prior for guessing parameter   gprior     = list(dist = "beta", params = c(5, 16)),# Prior: Beta(5,16) for g   Quadrature = c(49, 6),                              # 49 quadrature points from -6 to 6   group.mean = 0,   group.var  = 1,                                     # Fixed latent ability: N(0,1)   EmpHist    = TRUE,                                  # Estimate empirical ability distribution   Etol       = 1e-3,                                  # E-step convergence tolerance   MaxE       = 500)                                   # Max EM iterations  # Summarize estimation results irtQ::summary(mod_ref)  # Extract item parameter estimates est_ref <- mod_ref$par.est print(est_ref)  ##------------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## 2. Pretest item calibration using Fixed Item Parameter Calibration (FIPC) ##------------------------------------------------------------------------------  ## Step 1: Prepare item metadata for both fixed operational items and pretest items # Define anchor item positions (items to be fixed) fixed_pos <- c(1:40)  # Specify IDs, models, and categories for 15 pretest items # Includes 12 3PLM and 3 GRM items (each GRM has 5 categories) new_ids <- paste0("New_I", 1:15) new_models <- c(rep("3PLM", 12), rep("GRM", 3)) new_cats <- c(rep(2, 12), rep(5, 3))  # Construct item metadata using `shape_df_fipc()`. See Details of `shape_df_fipc()` # for more information # First 40 items are anchor items (fixed); last 15 are pretest (freely estimated) meta_fipc <- irtQ::shape_df_fipc(x = est_ref, fix.loc = fixed_pos, item.id = new_ids,                                  cats = new_cats, model = new_models)  ## Step 2: Prepare response data for the new test form # Generate latent abilities for 2,000 new examinees from N(0.5, 1.3^2) set.seed(21) theta_new <- rnorm(2000, mean = 0.5, sd = 1.3)  # Simulate response data using true item parameters and true abilities data_new <- irtQ::simdat(x = x_new, theta = theta_new, D = 1)  ## Step 3: Calibrate pretest items using FIPC # Fit 3PLM to dichotomous and GRM to polytomous items # Fix first 40 items and freely estimate the remaining 15 pretest items mod_fipc <- irtQ::est_irt(   x           = meta_fipc,                     # Combined item metadata   data        = data_new,                      # Response data   D           = 1,                             # Scaling constant   use.gprior  = TRUE,                          # Use prior for guessing parameter   gprior      = list(dist = "beta", params = c(5, 16)),  # Prior: Beta(5,16) for g   Quadrature  = c(49, 6),                      # 49 quadrature points from -6 to 6   EmpHist     = TRUE,                          # Estimate empirical ability distribution   Etol        = 1e-3,                          # E-step convergence tolerance   MaxE        = 500,                           # Max EM iterations   fipc        = TRUE,                          # Enable FIPC   fipc.method = "MEM",                         # Use Multiple EM cycles   fix.loc     = c(1:40))                       # Anchor item positions to fix  # Summarize estimation results irtQ::summary(mod_fipc)  # Extract item parameter estimates est_new_fipc <- mod_fipc$par.est print(est_new_fipc)  # Plot estimated empirical distribution of ability emphist <- irtQ::getirt(mod_fipc, what="weights") plot(emphist$weight ~ emphist$theta, xlab="Theta", ylab="Density", type = "h")   ##------------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## 3. Pretest item calibration using Fixed Ability Parameter Calibration (FAPC) ##------------------------------------------------------------------------------  ## Step 1: Prepare response data and ability estimates # In FAPC, ability estimates are assumed known and fixed. # Estimate abilities for new examinees using the first 40 fixed operational (anchor) items only. # Pretest items are not used for scoring, as their parameters are not yet calibrated.  # Estimate abilities using ML method via `irtQ::est_score()` # Based on fixed anchor item parameters and corresponding responses score_ml <- irtQ::est_score(   x      = est_ref,            # Metadata with operational item parameters   data   = data_new[, 1:40],   # Responses to anchor items   D      = 1,                  # Scaling constant   method = "ML",               # Scoring method: Maximum Likelihood   range  = c(-5, 5))           # Scoring bounds  # Extract estimated abilities theta_est <- score_ml$est.theta  ## Step 2: Calibrate pretest items using FAPC # Only the 15 pretest items are included in the calibration mod_fapc <- irtQ::est_item(   data       = data_new[, 41:55],                      # Responses to pretest items   score      = theta_est,                              # Fixed ability estimates   D          = 1,                                       # Scaling constant   model      = c(rep("3PLM", 12), rep("GRM", 3)),       # Item models   cats       = c(rep(2, 12), rep(5, 3)),                # Score categories   item.id    = paste0("New_I", 1:15),                   # Item IDs   use.gprior = TRUE,                                    # Use prior for guessing parameter   gprior     = list(dist = "beta", params = c(5, 16))   # Prior: Beta(5,16) for g )  # Summarize estimation results irtQ::summary(mod_fapc)  # Extract item parameter estimates est_new_fapc <- mod_fapc$par.est print(est_new_fapc)

text: compute \(\chi^2\) \(G^2\) item fit statistics, group.method argument determines ability scale divided groups: "equal.width": Examinees grouped intervals equal width along ability scale. "equal.freq": Examinees grouped group contains (approximately) number individuals. Note "equal.freq" guarantee exactly equal frequencies across groups, since grouping based quantiles. dividing ability scale intervals compute \(\chi^2\) \(G^2\) fit statistics, intervals : Wide enough ensure group contains sufficient number examinees (avoid unstable estimates), Narrow enough ensure examinees within group relatively homogeneous ability (Hambleton et al., 1991). Use n.width change number groups (default 10). reference: Yen (1981) used 10 groups approximately equal size, Bock (1960) allowed flexibility number groups. loc.theta = "average", expected probabilities group evaluated average ability estimate group. probability point approximates average model probabilities examinees group (e.g., Yen, 1981). Regarding degrees freedom (df), let \(G\) number ability groups collapsing, \(K\) number score categories, \(m\) number item parameters: \(\chi^2\) statistic approximately chi-square distributed \(G(K - 1) - m\) degrees freedom, \(G - m\) dichotomous item (Ames & Penfield, 2015). \(G^2\) statistic approximately chi-square distributed \(G(K - 1)\) degrees freedom, \(G\) dichotomous item (Ames & Penfield, 2015; Muraki & Bock, 2003). number item parameters \(m\) determined IRT model item: 1 1PLM, 2 2PLM, 3 3PLM, number score categories \(K\) GRM GPCM; item listed pcm.loc \(m = K - 1\), item labeled "DRM" counted 3PLM item. also applies est_irt est_item objects: parameters fixed estimation (example, fix.g = TRUE, items fixed FIPC) still counted, GPCM items estimated fix..gpcm = TRUE counted PCM items given pcm.loc. degrees freedom remain \(\chi^2\) collapsing (df.X2 0 less), crit.val.X2 p.X2 NA, warning names item. Responses data must integer scores 0 number score categories minus 1, one column per item. Character factor responses read numbers, logical responses 0 1, responses stop function error. ability group \(j\) \(N_j\) examinees, let \(O_{jk}\) \(E_{jk}\) observed proportion model-expected probability score category \(k\) theta point group (see loc.theta). statistics \(\chi^2 = \sum_j \sum_k N_j (O_{jk} - E_{jk})^2 / E_{jk}\) \(G^2 = 2 \sum_j \sum_k N_j O_{jk} \log(O_{jk} / E_{jk})\), cells \(O_{jk} = 0\) add nothing \(G^2\). dichotomous item, \(\chi^2\) form Yen's (1981) \(Q_1\) statistic \(\sum_j N_j (O_j - E_j)^2 / [E_j (1 - E_j)]\). standardized residual cell collapsing \((O_{jk} - E_{jk}) / \sqrt{E_{jk} (1 - E_{jk}) / N_j}\). Infit outfit use category scores \(0, \ldots, K - 1\). examinee \(n\), residual \(r_n = x_n - E(X \mid \theta_n)\) variance \(W_n = \sum_k (k - E(X \mid \theta_n))^2 P_k(\theta_n)\), \(\theta_n\) ability estimate score. Outfit unweighted mean \(\sum_n (r_n^2 / W_n) / N\), infit variance-weighted mean \(\sum_n r_n^2 / \sum_n W_n\). title: Pseudo-Count D2 Method for Item Parameter Drift Detection — pcd2
text: pseudo-count \(D^{2}\) statistic quantifies item parameter drift (IPD) computing, across quadrature points, weighted squared differences observed pseudo-proportion correct responses proportion expected item bank parameters, weighted pseudo-counts. observed pseudo-counts obtained posterior distribution examinee's ability, expected proportions probabilities correct response computed item bank parameters (Stone, 2000). pseudo-count \(D^{2}\) statistic calculated : $$ D^{2}_{PC} = \sum_{k=1}^{Q} \left( \frac{r_{0k} + r_{1k}}{N}\right) \left( \frac{r_{1k}}{r_{0k} + r_{1k}} - E_{1k} \right)^2 $$ \(Q\) number quadrature points, \(r_{0k}\) \(r_{1k}\) pseudo-counts incorrect correct responses quadrature point \(k\) (sums examinees' posterior probabilities point examinees response), \(E_{1k}\) probability correct response point \(k\) item bank parameters, \(N\) number examinees responded item. Critical Value (crit.val): crit.val argument specifies threshold used flag item exhibiting potential parameter drift. item's pseudo-count \(D^{2}\) value greater equal threshold, item flagged. crit.val = NULL, function reports raw statistic without flagging. Minimum Response Count (min.resp): min.resp argument sets lower bound number responses required item included analysis. Items fewer responses min.resp automatically excluded replacing responses NA. avoids unreliable estimates based small sample sizes. Purification Procedure: Although Cappaert et al. (2018) incorporate purification method, pcd2() implements optional iterative purification process similar Lim et al. (2022). purify = TRUE crit.val provided: procedure begins identifying items flagged drift using initial pseudo-count \(D^{2}\) statistics. subsequent iteration, item highest flagged pseudo-count \(D^{2}\) value removed item set, statistics recalculated using remaining items. process continues additional items flagged number iterations reaches max.iter. max.iter reached convergence, warning issued, items flagged last iteration added flagged set, complete set FALSE. every item flagged, procedure stops warning, item left analyze, items returned flagged, complete FALSE. flagged items statistics saved, convergence status reported. process reduces influence already-flagged items posterior distributions used remaining items.

data, crit.val = 0.002, purify = TRUE) #>   # \donttest{ ## -- Example 3: CAT-based IPD detection using simIPD -------------------------- ## ## The pseudo-count D2 statistic has no closed-form null distribution. ## Following Cappaert et al. (2018), the critical value is estimated ## empirically via bootstrap: ##   (1) Select items that are not suspected of IPD (anchor items). ##   (2) Compute D2 for the whole item pool from all responses, and take ##       the D2 values of the anchor items as the null distribution. ##   (3) Resample the null distribution with replacement, take the 95th ##       percentile of each bootstrap sample, and average the percentiles ##       to obtain the critical value. ##   (4) Run pcd2() with this critical value. ## ## The simIPD dataset provides: ##   item_par  : original 360-item pool (3PLM, irtQ format) ##   foc_resp  : focal group CAT responses (N = 3,000; TL = 30; ~92% NA) ##   key_item  : indices of 90 highly-exposed key items (IPD analysis targets) ##   item.skip : indices of 270 non-key items (excluded from analysis) ##   ipd_item  : 18 truly drifted items (ground truth; a & b each -0.5) ## -----------------------------------------------------------------------------  data(simIPD)  ## -- Step 1. Select anchor items for bootstrap ----------------------------- ## Select items that (a) have at least min_resp_anchor observed responses ## and (b) are not suspected of IPD. In practice, exclude the items you ## suspect to have drifted; here the ground truth (simIPD$ipd_item) is ## excluded for illustration. ## The minimum response count follows Lim & Han (2026); it is a practical ## addition to the procedure of Cappaert et al. (2018), who did not set such ## a criterion. In a CAT pool with uneven exposure, items with few responses ## have large D2 values that inflate the tail of the null distribution. For ## the simIPD data, the critical value computed below is about 0.034 when ## all items with at least one response are used, about 0.008 with at least ## 50 responses, about 0.006 with at least 100, and about 0.004 with at ## least 300. min_resp_anchor <- 300 n_resp          <- colSums(!is.na(simIPD$foc_resp))   # observed responses per item anchor_items    <- setdiff(which(n_resp >= min_resp_anchor), simIPD$ipd_item)  ## -- Step 2. Compute D2 for the whole pool and keep the anchor items ------- ## D2 is computed once from all items and responses, so that the posterior ## ability distributions are the same as in the final analysis (Step 4). ## A warning lists the pool items that were never administered. pcd2_all  <- pcd2(   x    = simIPD$item_par,   data = simIPD$foc_resp,   D    = 1.7 ) #> Warning: Item(s) 17, 19, 22, 24, 27, 30, 32, 34, 44, 47, 50, 54, 56, 65, 73, 76, 77, 82, 86, 93, 102, 105, 108, 111, 112, 120, 122, 131, 137, 140, 144, 155, 156, 164, 165, 174, 176, 182, 193, 196, 201, 206, 219, 222, 223, 225, 232, 241, 255, 265, 269, 271, 278, 279, 284, 286, 289, 291, 292, 293, 295, 305, 313, 315, 316, 339, 342, 343, 344, 345, 352, 353, 359 have no response data. pcd2_null <- pcd2_all$no_purify$ipd_stat$pcd2[anchor_items]  ## -- Step 3. Bootstrap critical value (Cappaert et al., 2018) -------------- ## For each bootstrap iteration: resample the null D2 values with replacement ## (the sample size equals the number of anchor items) and take the 95th ## percentile. The critical value is the mean of these percentiles. ## n_boots = 500: reduced for demo speed; use 10,000 in practice for a ##   stable critical value estimate. set.seed(2024) n_boots <- 500  crit_val <- mean(vapply(   X   = seq_len(n_boots),   FUN = function(b) {     stats::quantile(sample(x = pcd2_null, size = length(pcd2_null), replace = TRUE),                     probs = 0.95)   },   FUN.VALUE = numeric(1) ))  cat("Bootstrap critical value (alpha = 0.05):", round(crit_val, 6), "
") #> Bootstrap critical value (alpha = 0.05): 0.004059   ## -- Step 4. Run PCD2 with the bootstrap critical value + purification -- ## The statistics of the first analysis (pcd2_result$no_purify) are the same ## as those of pcd2_all for the analyzed items, since the same responses are ## used. The same warning about the items that were never administered ## appears. pcd2_result <- pcd2(   x         = simIPD$item_par,   data      = simIPD$foc_resp,   D         = 1.7,   item.skip = simIPD$item.skip,   crit.val  = crit_val,   purify    = TRUE,   max.iter  = 30 ) #> Warning: Item(s) 17, 19, 22, 24, 27, 30, 32, 34, 44, 47, 50, 54, 56, 65, 73, 76, 77, 82, 86, 93, 102, 105, 108, 111, 112, 120, 122, 131, 137, 140, 144, 155, 156, 164, 165, 174, 176, 182, 193, 196, 201, 206, 219, 222, 223, 225, 232, 241, 255, 265, 269, 271, 278, 279, 284, 286, 289, 291, 292, 293, 295, 305, 313, 315, 316, 339, 342, 343, 344, 345, 352, 353, 359 have no response data. #> Purification started...  #>   Iteration: 1  Iteration: 2  Iteration: 3  Iteration: 4  Iteration: 5  Iteration: 6  Iteration: 7  Iteration: 8  Iteration: 9  Iteration: 10  Iteration: 11  Iteration: 12  Iteration: 13  Iteration: 14  Iteration: 15  Iteration: 16  Iteration: 17  Iteration: 18  Iteration: 19  #> Purification is finished.   ## -- Step 5. Compare detected items to ground truth -------------------- detected <- pcd2_result$with_purify$ipd_item cat("Truly drifted items (ground truth):", simIPD$ipd_item, "
") #> Truly drifted items (ground truth): 26 42 55 58 97 129 138 145 149 181 184 203 242 246 252 310 334 336  cat("PCD2-detected items:               ", detected, "
") #> PCD2-detected items:                26 42 55 58 97 129 138 145 149 181 184 203 236 242 246 252 310 334 336  cat("True positives:", sum(detected %in% simIPD$ipd_item), "of",     length(simIPD$ipd_item), "
") #> True positives: 18 of 18  # }

text: function computes three RDIF statistics item: \(RDIF_{R}\), \(RDIF_{S}\), \(RDIF_{RS}\) (Lim & Choe, 2023; Lim et al., 2022). \(RDIF_{R}\) primarily captures differences raw residuals two groups, typically associated uniform DIF. \(RDIF_{S}\) primarily captures differences squared residuals, typically associated nonuniform DIF. \(RDIF_{RS}\) jointly considers types differences capable detecting uniform nonuniform DIF.

title: Residual-based Item Parameter Drift (RIPD) Detection Framework — ripd
code:
## --- RIPD Example: Detecting IPD in CAT --------------------------------- ## ## Background (Lim & Han, 2026): ##   In CAT-based IPD detection using RIPD, the reference group is ##   "synthetic": it is created by re-administering a CAT to examinees whose ##   true abilities are set equal to the focal group's ML theta estimates, ##   using the ORIGINAL (pre-drift) item parameters. This eliminates the ##   need for recalibration and makes RIPD directly applicable to ##   operational CAT settings. ## ## The simIPD dataset contains: ##   - foc_resp / foc_score : focal group CAT responses + ML theta estimates ##                            (IPD items: a and b each drifted by -0.5) ##   - ref_resp / ref_score : synthetic reference group CAT responses + ML ##                            theta estimates (original parameters, 1F size) ##   - item_par  : original (non-drifted) 360-item pool in irtQ format ##   - key_item  : indices of 90 key items (highly exposed in CAT) ##   - item.skip : indices of 270 non-key items (excluded from RIPD) ##   - ipd_item  : indices of 18 truly drifted items (ground truth) ## -------------------------------------------------------------------------  data(simIPD)  ## Step 1. Combine focal and synthetic reference group data ##         (the row order does not matter as long as group matches the rows) data  <- rbind(simIPD$ref_resp,  simIPD$foc_resp) score <- c(simIPD$ref_score,     simIPD$foc_score) group <- c(rep(0, nrow(simIPD$ref_resp)),   # 0 = reference            rep(1, nrow(simIPD$foc_resp)))   # 1 = focal  ## Step 2. Run RIPD without purification ##         item.skip excludes the 270 non-key items from analysis ripd_result <- ripd(   x          = simIPD$item_par,   data       = data,   score      = score,   group      = group,   focal.name = 1,           # focal group is coded as 1   item.skip  = simIPD$item.skip,   D          = 1.7,   alpha      = 0.05,   purify     = FALSE,   method     = "ML",   range      = c(-5, 5) )  ## Step 3. Compare the items flagged by RIPD_RS to the ground truth detected <- ripd_result$no_purify$ipd_item$ripdrs cat("Truly drifted items (ground truth):", simIPD$ipd_item, "
") #> Truly drifted items (ground truth): 26 42 55 58 97 129 138 145 149 181 184 203 242 246 252 310 334 336  cat("RIPD_RS-flagged items:             ", detected, "
") #> RIPD_RS-flagged items:              26 55 58 97 129 130 138 145 149 181 184 203 215 231 236 242 246 252 277 310 312 334 336 351 354  cat("True positives:", sum(detected %in% simIPD$ipd_item), "of",     length(simIPD$ipd_item), "
") #> True positives: 17 of 18   ## Step 4. Purification (not run: it takes several minutes because the ##         abilities of the examinees are re-estimated at every iteration) ## ##   ripd_purified <- ripd( ##     x = simIPD$item_par, data = data, score = score, group = group, ##     focal.name = 1, item.skip = simIPD$item.skip, D = 1.7, alpha = 0.05, ##     purify = TRUE, purify.by = "ripdrs", max.iter = 30, ##     method = "ML", range = c(-5, 5) ##   ) ##   print(ripd_purified, what = "with_purify")  ## -- Note on reference group size ----------------------------------------- ## This example uses a 1F reference group (n_ref = n_foc = 3,000). ## In practice, a larger reference group improves detection power; ## Lim and Han (2026) suggest at least 8F to 10F. To create, for example, ## an 8F reference group, replicate the focal ability estimates and run ## the same CAT simulation with the original item parameters using a CAT ## simulation program (irtQ does not provide one): ## ##   theta_8F <- rep(simIPD$foc_score, times = 8)   # 24,000 examinees ##   # simulate a CAT for theta_8F with simIPD$item_par, then call ripd() ##   # with the simulated responses and final ability estimates ## -------------------------------------------------------------------------

code: # Examples below will run if the flexMIRT software is installed # in the default directory "C:/Program Files/flexMIRT3". # Otherwise, specify the directory where flexMIRT is installed # using the 'dir.flex' argument.  if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # (1) Run a single syntax file # Copy an example syntax file and its data file to a temporary folder ext <- system.file("extdata", package = "irtQ") file.copy(file.path(ext, c("2PLM_example.flexmirt", "g341-19.dat")),           tempdir()) file.syntax <- file.path(tempdir(), "2PLM_example.flexmirt")  # Run flexMIRT to estimate item parameters for the 2PL model run_flexmirt(file.syntax = file.syntax, dir.flex = NULL,              show.output.on.console = TRUE)  # Read the item parameter file written by flexMIRT out.file <- file.path(tempdir(), "2PLM_example-prm.txt") bring.flexmirt(out.file, type = "par")  # (2) Run multiple syntax files # Copy two example syntax files and the data file to a temporary folder file.copy(file.path(ext, c("3PLM_example.flexmirt", "g341-19.dat")),           tempdir()) file.syntax1 <- file.path(tempdir(), "2PLM_example.flexmirt") file.syntax2 <- file.path(tempdir(), "3PLM_example.flexmirt")  # Run flexMIRT to estimate item parameters for both models run_flexmirt(file.syntax = c(file.syntax1, file.syntax2), dir.flex = NULL,              show.output.on.console = FALSE)  # Read the item parameter files written by flexMIRT out.file1 <- file.path(tempdir(), "2PLM_example-prm.txt") out.file2 <- file.path(tempdir(), "3PLM_example-prm.txt") bring.flexmirt(out.file1, type = "par") bring.flexmirt(out.file2, type = "par") } # }

code: # A small 5-examinee, 3-item toy example with a blank and a double-mark raw <- data.frame(   V1 = c("1", "2", NA, "1", "3"),   V2 = c("4", "4", "4", "2,4", "4"),   V3 = c("2", "1", "3", "3", NA) ) key <- c(1, 4, 3) out <- score_resp(data = raw, key = key) out$scored #>   V1 V2 V3 #> 1  1  1  0 #> 2  0  1  0 #> 3  0  1  1 #> 4  1  0  1 #> 5  0  1  0 out$resp_summary #>   item key n n_correct n_wrong n_blank n_double n_invalid pct_blank pct_double #> 1   V1   1 5         2       3       1        0         0        20          0 #> 2   V2   4 5         4       1       0        1         0         0         20 #> 3   V3   3 5         2       3       1        0         0        20          0  # Same data, but omitted responses are coded as "9" instead of NA raw2 <- data.frame(   V1 = c("1", "2", "9", "1", "3"),   V2 = c("4", "4", "4", "2,4", "4"),   V3 = c("2", "1", "3", "3", "9") ) out2 <- score_resp(data = raw2, key = key, missing = "9") identical(out$scored, out2$scored) #> [1] TRUE  # A letter-coded (A-E) example, including a double-marked response and a # lowercase response ("a"), which is matched case-insensitively raw3 <- data.frame(   V1 = c("A", "B", NA, "a", "C"),   V2 = c("D", "D", "D", "B,D", "D"),   V3 = c("B", "A", "C", "C", NA) ) key3 <- c("A", "D", "C") out3 <- score_resp(data = raw3, key = key3) out3$scored #>   V1 V2 V3 #> 1  1  1  0 #> 2  0  1  0 #> 3  0  1  1 #> 4  1  0  1 #> 5  0  1  0  # A mixed-format test: item 1 is numerically coded, items 2-3 are # letter-coded; the coding scheme is inferred separately for each item # from its own key value raw4 <- data.frame(   V1 = c("1", "2", "1", "1", "3"),   V2 = c("D", "D", "D", "B,D", "D"),   V3 = c("B", "A", "C", "C", NA) ) key4 <- c(1, "D", "C") out4 <- score_resp(data = raw4, key = key4) out4$scored #>   V1 V2 V3 #> 1  1  1  0 #> 2  0  1  0 #> 3  1  1  1 #> 4  1  0  1 #> 5  0  1  0  # A full five-option (A-E) multiple-choice item, scored against key "C" raw5 <- data.frame(   V1 = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "c") ) key5 <- c("C") out5 <- score_resp(data = raw5, key = key5) out5$scored #>   V1 #> 1  0 #> 2  0 #> 3  1 #> 4  0 #> 5  0 #> 6  1  # A general-label-coded example using non-Latin option labels: the Korean # syllables romanized "ga"/"na"/"da"/"ra"/"ma", written here with \uXXXX # escapes for ASCII portability. Because these labels are neither numbers # nor Latin letters, they are handled by the general label-coding scheme # described in Details raw6 <- data.frame(   V1 = c("\uAC00", "\uB098", "\uB2E4", "\uB2E4", NA) # ga, na, da, da, NA ) key6 <- c("\uB2E4") # da out6 <- score_resp(data = raw6, key = key6) out6$scored #>   V1 #> 1  0 #> 2  0 #> 3  1 #> 4  1 #> 5  0

text: simulated dataset designed illustrate use ripd pcd2 functions detecting item parameter drift (IPD) computerized adaptive testing (CAT). dataset represents one replication CAT-based IPD simulation study 5% 360-item pool (18 items) discrimination () difficulty (b) parameters drift downward 0.5, 30-item adaptive test drift affected focal group examinees (100% drift exposure condition Lim & Han, 2026). data reflect workflow IPD detection using residual-based IPD (RIPD) framework (Lim & Han, 2026): focal group examinees takes CAT using drifted item pool, synthetic reference group created re-running CAT focal group's ability estimates true abilities original (non-drifted) item parameters. RIPD statistics used detect items drifted two groups.

title: Simulated CAT Data for Item Parameter Drift (IPD) Detection — simIPD
text: named list eight elements: item_par data frame 360 rows 6 columns containing original (pre-drift) item metadata (columns: id, cats, model, par.1, par.2, par.3). items follow 3PLM. key_item numeric vector length 90 giving row indices (item_par) key items, , items identified preliminary CAT simulation frequently administered therefore relevant IPD analysis. item.skip integer vector length 270 giving row indices non-key items excluded IPD analysis (.e., complement key_item 1:360). Pass vector item.skip argument ripd() pcd2(). ipd_item numeric vector length 18 giving row indices items subjected IPD manipulation. 18 items (5% 360-item pool) discrimination () difficulty (b) parameters decreased 0.5. 18 items members key_item. foc_resp numeric matrix dimensions 3000 x 360 containing focal group CAT response data. row one examinee; column corresponds item item_par (column names item IDs). CAT administers 30 items per examinee, approximately 92% entries NA. Responses generated using drifted item parameters (drifted parameters used every focal group examinee received IPD item). foc_score numeric vector length 3000 containing focal group final maximum likelihood (ML) ability estimates obtained CAT, bounded range -5 5. ref_resp numeric matrix dimensions 3000 x 360 containing synthetic reference group CAT response data (examinee also 30 observed responses 92% entries NA). reference group constructed : (1) using foc_score true ability values (1F condition, .e., reference group size focal group); (2) generating item responses original (non-drifted) item parameters; (3) running independent CAT simulation. synthetic reference group mirrors construction described Lim & Han (2026). ref_score numeric vector length 3000 containing synthetic reference group final ML ability estimates, bounded range -5 5.

title: Simulated CAT Data for Item Parameter Drift (IPD) Detection — simIPD
text: Simulation conditions: Item pool: 360 three-parameter logistic model (3PLM) items Test length: 30 items per examinee Item selection: maximum Fisher information (MFI), fade-away exposure control method (maximum exposure rate 0.30) initial abilities drawn \(U(-1, 1)\) Focal group: \(n = 3{,}000\); true abilities drawn \(N(0, 1)\) Reference group: \(n = 3{,}000\) (1F); true abilities = foc_score IPD items: 18 (5% 360), randomly drawn key_item IPD manipulation: b decreased 0.50 Interim scoring: EAP; final scoring: ML Scaling factor: \(D = 1.7\) Random seed: 2024 Note reference group size: 1F reference group (size focal group) used compactness. practice, larger synthetic reference groups improve RIPD detection power; Lim Han (2026) suggest reference group least 8 10 times focal group size (8F 10F). larger reference group can created replicating focal ability estimates, e.g., rep(foc_score, times = 8) 8F group, re-running CAT simulation original item parameters using CAT simulation program.

title: Simulate Response Data — simdat
text: two ways generate simulated response data. first providing data frame item metadata using argument x. data frame must follow specific structure: first column contain item IDs, second column contain number unique score categories item, third column specify IRT model fitted item. Available IRT models : "1PLM", "2PLM", "3PLM", "DRM" dichotomous item data "GRM" "GPCM" polytomous item data Note "DRM" serves general label covering dichotomous IRT models (.e., "1PLM", "2PLM", "3PLM"), "GRM" "GPCM" represent graded response model (generalized) partial credit model, respectively. subsequent columns contain item parameters specified models. dichotomous items, fourth, fifth, sixth columns represent item discrimination (slope), item difficulty, item guessing parameters, respectively. "1PLM" "2PLM" specified third column, sixth column ignored can NA. polytomous items, item discrimination (slope) parameter appear fourth column, item difficulty (threshold) parameters category boundaries occupy fifth last columns. number unique score categories differs across items, unused parameter cells filled NAs. irtQ package, threshold parameters GPCM item \(b_v = \beta - \tau_v\), overall item location minus threshold score category. GPCM item K unique score categories requires K - 1 threshold parameters, term lowest score category fixed 0 supplied. example, GPCM item five score categories requires four threshold parameters. example data frame single-format test shown : example data frame mixed-format test shown : See IRT Models section irtQ-package documentation details IRT models used irtQ package. convenient way create data frame argument x using function shape_df(). second approach specify item parameters directly instead x (see Examples). case, theta cats required, along .drm b.drm dichotomous items .prm, d.prm, pr.model polytomous items. g.drm argument required simulating dichotomous item responses 3PL model. can omitted entirely dichotomous items follow 1PL 2PL model. However, test includes mixture 1PL, 2PL, 3PL items, g.drm vector must specified dichotomous items, using NA non-3PL items. example, test consists four dichotomous items first two follow 3PL model third fourth follow 1PL 2PL models respectively, g.drm = c(0.2, 0.1, NA, NA) used. dichotomous items, element cats set 2. polytomous items, number unique score categories specified cats. simulating data mixed-format test, important specify cats correct item order. example, suppose responses simulated 10 examinees across 5 items, including 3 dichotomous items 2 polytomous items (3 categories), second fourth items polytomous. case, cats = c(2, 3, 2, 3, 2) used. Furthermore, two polytomous items modeled using graded response model generalized partial credit model, respectively, pr.model = c("GRM", "GPCM").

text: x data frame item metadata (e.g., item parameters, number categories, model types) single group, list data frames multiple groups. Default c(0, 1). rePar Logical. Indicates parameters x given. TRUE (default), x taken hold flexMIRT slope-intercept values: slopes, intercepts, logits guessing parameters, GPCM items scoring function intercept values nominal model; written . FALSE, x taken hold irtQ item metadata (slopes, difficulty step parameters, guessing parameters), converted flexMIRT parameterization. Item metadata irtQ (example, shape_df() est_irt()) must written rePar = FALSE. Note meaning reverse rePar argument bring.flexmirt(), TRUE converts values file irtQ metadata. mgroup logical value indicating whether file includes multiple groups. Default FALSE. group.name character vector group names. NULL, group names automatically generated (e.g., "Group1", "Group2", ...).

Create a "-prm.txt" file for a single group ##    using the simulated CAT data # 1-(1) Extract the item metadata x <- simCAT_MX$item.prm  # 1-(2) Set the name of the "-prm.txt" file temp_prm <- file.path(tempdir(), "single_group_temp-prm.txt")  # 1-(3) Write the "-prm.txt" file write.flexmirt(x, file = temp_prm, norm.pop = c(0, 1), rePar = FALSE)  # 1-(4) Read the file back and compare the item parameters x_back <- bring.flexmirt(file = temp_prm, type = "par")$Group1$full_df head(x_back) #>   id cats model     par.1       par.2 par.3 par.4 #> 1 V1    2  2PLM 0.9664715 -0.84085552    NA    NA #> 2 V2    2  2PLM 0.9152754  1.38435940    NA    NA #> 3 V3    2  2PLM 1.3454796 -1.25549187    NA    NA #> 4 V4    2  2PLM 0.7925184  0.07014276    NA    NA #> 5 V5    2  2PLM 1.0862914  1.71144078    NA    NA #> 6 V6    2  2PLM 1.1311496 -0.60290796    NA    NA max(abs(as.matrix(x[, 4:7]) - as.matrix(x_back[, 4:7])), na.rm = TRUE) #> [1] 1.70888e-07  ## 2. Create a "-prm.txt" file for multiple groups ##    using simulated multi-group data # 2-(1) Extract the item metadata x <- simMG$item.prm  # Set the name of the "-prm.txt" file temp_prm <- file.path(tempdir(), "mg_group_temp-prm1.txt")  # Write the "-prm.txt" file, giving the mean and variance of each group write.flexmirt(x,   file = temp_prm, norm.pop = list(c(0, 1), c(0.5, 0.64), c(-0.3, 1.69)),   rePar = FALSE, mgroup = TRUE, group.name = c("GR1", "GR2", "GR3") )  # Or write the "-prm.txt" file so that # all groups share the same ability distribution # and group names are generated automatically temp_prm <- file.path(tempdir(), "mg_group_temp-prm2.txt") write.flexmirt(x,   file = temp_prm, norm.pop = c(0, 1),   rePar = FALSE, mgroup = TRUE, group.name = NULL ) # }

title: irtQ 1.1.0
text: Added unit test suite using testthat 3rd edition (testthat >= 3.0.0). Tests cover core functions including drm(), prm(), est_irt(), est_score(), est_mg(), rdif(), crdif(), catsib(), relevant tests across dichotomous, polytomous, mixed-format item scenarios (355 tests total). Added new function, ripd(), implements Residual-based Item Parameter Drift (RIPD) detection framework. function computes three RIPD statistics: RIPDRRIPD_R, RIPDSRIPD_S, RIPDRSRIPD_{RS} (one item). RIPDRRIPD_R captures uniform item parameter drift (IPD) via differences mean raw residuals groups, RIPDSRIPD_S captures nonuniform IPD via differences mean squared residuals, RIPDRSRIPD_{RS} combined chi-square-based statistic sensitive types drift. optional purification procedure also supported.
